articles.title: Trump’s Cuba report borrowed heavily from my book on an anti-imperialist movement – but twisted the arguments
articles.author:
<name>Anne Garland Mahler, Professor and Director of Latin American Studies Program, University of Virginia</name>
      <foaf:homepage rdf:resource="https://theconversation.com/profiles/anne-garland-mahler-2752252"/>
paras: For decades after the Cuban Revolution’s victory in 1959, influential anticommunist circles in the United States claimed that Cuba’s communist government sowed social division and allied with left-wing groups to help defeat Washington during the Cold War.

This right-wing rhetoric has been revived in the Trump State Department’s July 20, 2026, report, “ Cuba: The Capital of 21st Century Communism .” In it, the administration seizes on the history of a movement called the Tricontinental – an alliance of liberation movements from around the world founded in 1966 – to make the unsubstantiated claim that the U.S. left is currently engaged in a Cuban conspiracy to destroy the U.S.

As a professor of Latin American studies at the University of Virginia, I wrote the first scholarly book on the Tricontinental movement , “From the Tricontinental to the Global South: Race, Radicalism, and Transnational Solidarity.”

The State Department’s report summarizes large portions of that book’s arguments without citation, particularly in its attention to the Tricontinental’s historical relationship with the U.S. Civil Rights Movement. The report also misrepresents a larger body of scholarship on the relationship between Cuba and the left wing in the U.S. The State Department didn’t respond to a request for comment on whether it had used my book as a source.

But while the report preserves the structure of my book’s historical arguments, it twists its interpretations and conclusions. The effect is to support the Trump administration’s false claim that Cuba has “backed an unprecedented wave of left-wing terrorism on American soil.”

The Tricontinental was officially known as the Organization of Solidarity with the Peoples of Africa, Asia, and Latin America, or OSPAAAL. It was formed in 1966 when self-determination movements from 82 countries came together in Havana for the Tricontinental Conference. Although some conference delegates were recognizable leaders of political parties – like Chile’s Salvador Allende and Guinea-Bissau’s Amílcar Cabral – most were lesser-known representatives of a variety of political organizations, including from the United States.

The OSPAAAL formed as the expansion into the Americas of the Afro-Asian Peoples’ Solidarity Organization (AAPSO) , founded in 1957 as an alternative power bloc to the U.S.-Soviet Cold War division. Seeking new global allies, Cuba joined the Afro-Asian bloc after Havana’s 1962 ousting from the Organization of American States. With Cuba’s joining of AAPSO to form OSPAAAL, leftist organizations and political figures from across Latin America and the U.S. also joined as members.

Yet the history of the Tricontinental had much deeper roots in Black political movements in the Americas. The original idea for the Tricontinental came from Afro-Cuban intellectual Walterio Carbonell , who had close links to trans-Atlantic Black activist networks. In the Tricontinental’s aim to bring together class- and race-based organizing, it responded to long-standing debates within those networks.

More than a conference or an alliance, the Tricontinental movement should be understood as a producer of political culture. For over four decades and in multiple languages, it distributed magazines, films, posters and other materials around the world. The Tricontinental became known for the artistically innovative films, posters and magazines that it published in English, Spanish, French and Arabic.

The OSPAAAL created a shared language and aesthetics for a wide range of anticolonial and anti-racist movements worldwide. Through its materials, the OSPAAAL played a pivotal role in generating international solidarity with the U.S. Civil Rights Movement as well as with the anti-apartheid struggle in South Africa. Black activists from the U.S., moreover, helped shape its vision.
Although the OSPAAAL continued to produce materials until its 2019 closure, it reached its peak in the 1960s and ‘70s and is primarily known today for its striking posters.

The Tricontinental movement was not a tool used by Cuba to “express hatred of the United States,” as argued by the Trump administration’s Cuba report. Instead, it differentiated its critique of the U.S. government’s military interventions in Vietnam or Cuba from its abiding support for the American people.

Tricontinental magazine and Tricontinental Bulletin often featured U.S. civil rights leaders and organizations and demonstrated a commitment to solidarity with the struggles of U.S. citizens to gain full rights and freedom.

Moreover, the OSPAAAL was an international, nongovernmental organization that did not belong solely to Cuba. Although Cuba played a central role in its operations, Tricontinental materials reflected a variety of leftist positions that did not always align perfectly with the Cuban government’s rhetoric.
And although the OSPAAAL was highly critical of U.S. military interventions in Latin America and elsewhere, its critique was not exclusively focused on the U.S.

To address the concerns of its diverse membership, the OSPAAAL defined its global enemy of “imperialism” broadly, encompassing forces of exploitation suffered by all members. For its membership, that included notions of settler colonialism , such as in land that became Israel and the occupied Palestinian territories; exploitation colonialism, such as in the former Portuguese colonies in Africa ; and strategies of economic domination that characterized U.S. policy toward Latin America and similar trends elsewhere.
Activists involved in the OSPAAAL also had varied positions toward Cuba’s communist government.

The Black Power activist Stokely Carmichael , who was invited to become a member of the OSPAAAL’s executive secretariat, developed a critical stance against the Cuban government’s restrictions on anti-racist political organizing within Cuba based on its claim that socialist reforms had ended structural racial inequalities on the island.

The North Carolina NAACP activist Robert F. Williams , who attended the Tricontinental Conference, developed similar viewpoints after living in Cuba from 1961-1965. While these activists eventually distanced themselves from the Cuban government, they continued to underscore the core tenets of the politics of Tricontinentalism in their writings.

The history of these Tricontinental activists is increasingly relevant today. For people like Carmichael or Williams, who devoted their lives to the struggle for freedom for all people, support for Cuban self-determination also required a critical engagement with the flaws of its government.
The White House Cuba report exemplifies the false binaries that predominate in discussions about Cuba on both the left and right.

The report falsely suggests that any group opposed to American intervention in Cuba is an imminent threat to the United States. Alternatively, due to the U.S. government’s long-term efforts to punish Cuba through economic embargo and attempted regime change, some sectors of the U.S. left view any criticism of Cuba’s government as an attack on its sovereignty.

The Tricontinental’s history offers a more nuanced and principled political position, one that opposes oppression in any form and that places self-determination for all people at the heart of its politics. The Trump administration’s use of that history for today’s policy toward Cuba is, I believe, mere political theater.

Anne Garland Mahler does not work for, consult, own shares in or receive funding from any company or organization that would benefit from this article, and has disclosed no relevant affiliations beyond their academic appointment.

articles.title: Children in a Faith-Healing Sect Keep Dying. The State Lets It Happen.
articles.author: Audrey Dutton
paras: A sheriff’s deputy opens the door of an Idaho farmhouse where a newborn baby has just died. It’s almost 10 p.m., but the house is filled with adults and children seated anywhere they can find a spot: in reclining chairs, on the wood-stove hearth, on a chest of drawers. Some of the women hold babies in their laps.
“Sorry,” the deputy whispers as the door creaks.
No one greets the officer. No one speaks or even looks at anyone else, casting their eyes instead at the floor or around the room.

The deputy’s video camera records as he walks through the front room and past a bedroom door adorned with children’s artwork. Inside the bedroom, newborn Malachi’s mother sits in a recliner. His body lies in her lap, covered by a blue blanket.

As people in uniform ask Malachi’s parents about his birth, death and the two days in between, members of the family’s church — one of at least four Followers of Christ churches in Idaho — watch from folding chairs. People come and go from the bedroom; one woman cradles a sleeping toddler.
Malachi died from pneumonia and bleeding lungs, according to an autopsy.
It would have been treatable with antibiotics and newborn care in a hospital, said doctors who reviewed his death records for ProPublica.

But Malachi’s parents belong to a faith-healing sect that doesn’t believe in medical care, based on a literal interpretation of several Bible verses. The Followers of Christ sect believes that God heals the faithful and that life and death must be left to God’s divine will.

When the coroner’s deputy lifted Malachi’s body to take it away that night in October 2023, there was no wailing or sobbing from his parents. Malachi’s father stood quietly as his mother hung her head and rested it in her hand.

A pediatrician who reviewed Malachi’s death records said a baby in his condition would have been gasping for air, turning blue from lack of oxygen and breathing so hard that the outline of his rib cage was visible.
It was the first time the coroner and sheriff sent their deputies out to that house, to interview those parents and document the slow suffocation of a newborn boy.
The next time was 13 months later, when their next newborn, Liam, died from the same treatable condition that killed his brother Malachi.

In any Idaho household not steeped in faith-healing, those two deaths would be investigated as crimes. Idaho law says parents can’t endanger, injure or neglect their children or let them suffer . To do so is a crime, and if the child dies as a result, the parent could be charged with manslaughter.

But those laws do not apply to children like Malachi and Liam. Since the 1970s, Idaho’s criminal and civil laws have allowed parents who belong to Followers of Christ and the state’s other faith-healing sects to pray rather than seek medical care as their children die.

Lawmakers in Oregon, where the same religious groups exist, removed the state’s faith-healing exception to child abuse laws nearly 30 years ago, countering the overwhelming pressure former Followers say parents face from their congregations. More parents chose to get medical care for their children after the change, Oregon prosecutors and detectives said.
Idaho lawmakers have chosen a different path.

Since 2014, they have rejected repeated efforts to dial back Idaho’s faith-healing exemption, instead crafting legislation to further limit the role of anyone but a parent when it comes to children’s health and safety. The state has codified “parental rights,” banned vaccine requirements in schools and childcare centers, and made parental consent a prerequisite for medical care of minors. Legislators also have tried to narrow the definition of “medical neglect” for all families to only the most life-threatening situations, but those attempts have failed.

Local and national media outlets have reported on deaths among Followers of Christ families in Idaho. ProPublica went further, enlisting the help of experts to determine which of those deaths could have been prevented.
ProPublica gathered death records from coroners and police in five Idaho counties and shared them with more than a dozen pediatricians and birthing specialists.
At least 15 babies and children from the faith-healing sect died between 2015 and 2025 from illnesses that doctors could have successfully treated, the experts concluded.

The estimate of preventable deaths is almost certainly an undercount. The experts could not evaluate six more deaths because coroner records were incomplete or unavailable. In another four cases, they couldn’t say with confidence whether medical care would have changed the outcome.
Separately, the experts identified numerous preventable losses of babies who died during birth or in utero very close to their due dates, cases that coroners labeled as stillbirths.

For some families like Liam and Malachi’s, the death of a child wasn’t a one-time tragedy: Records show at least five sets of parents have lost multiple children, a phenomenon that has not previously been reported.

None of the parents responded to letters or text messages from ProPublica, and one declined to comment during a brief phone call. (ProPublica is choosing not to identify them or use the children’s full names out of respect for their privacy.)
But Nathan Kangas, a patriarch in the sect’s Caldwell, Idaho, church, defended faith healing and its legal protection during an interview with ProPublica.

Children and babies can’t make their own decision to rely on faith healing. Kangas said their parents must keep them away from the doctor to set an example, so the young ones won’t be cursed later in life by turning to medicine.
Kangas lost his own wife and their last child during labor 23 years ago. Three of his 65 grandchildren also have died.

Asked why God would not want children to live full and healthy lives, Kangas said he had no answer but quoted a verse from the Book of Psalms: “Precious in the eyes of the Lord are the death of His saints.” The Followers believe that life on Earth is “a preparing ground,” Kangas said. He pointed to the Book of James, which tells people to “be afflicted and mourn and weep” and “let your laughter be turned to mourning.”
“It isn’t necessarily that we’re supposed to have a joyous life here,” Kangas said. “It’s actually quite the opposite.”
Some outsiders take a very different view.

Canyon County Sheriff Kieran Donahue, one of the most vocal opponents of Idaho’s faith-healing laws, has sent deputies to follow up on the deaths of at least 10 Followers’ children and infants since he took office in 2013.
“This is needless,” Donahue said. “This shouldn’t be happening.”
David Peterman, a retired Idaho pediatrician, reviewed the deaths of 18 infants and children at ProPublica’s request.

Peterman saw patients for 40 years and did his residency at a center that offered special training in child abuse and neglect. He said the vast majority of the deaths he reviewed for ProPublica “are the result of neglect and unequivocally preventable.” (He couldn’t tell whether a few deaths were preventable, and he surmised that one infant had a fatal, untreatable chromosomal defect.) He said it is “beyond comprehension” that the Idaho Legislature has refused to change the law.
“How is this tolerable?” he said. “I don’t understand how there could be an exception in Idaho law that allows for these children to die.”

Maicy was 16 years old but the size of a third grader: 62 pounds and just shy of 4 feet tall. She had suffered from a constellation of ailments: stomach irritation, severe anemia, erratic menstrual periods, a blocked artery, thickened aorta and thinning hair. An autopsy after she died on New Year’s Day 2019 traced it all back to a benign, treatable pituitary tumor.

Doctors who reviewed her death records said her stunted growth would have been obvious earlier in childhood, when her tumor could have been diagnosed and treated. Instead, it sent her body into a hormonal tailspin that destroyed her organs. She died in bed, lying on a towel and absorbent pad, wearing a diaper under her sweatpants and a T-shirt that read “LOVE.”

Some of the children who died preventable deaths over a decade were sick for hours or days; others endured months or — in Maicy’s case — years of disease. Most died in their parents’ arms. Many would have experienced pain and distress from their untreated conditions, the healthcare professionals consulted by ProPublica said.

“I don’t know how to come to terms with that,” said Beth Hartman, an Idaho midwife and former chair of the state’s midwifery licensing board. “Because when you see respiratory distress, and when you have seen a person pass, it’s not pretty. They don’t just close their eyes.”

In America at large, the risk that a child will die is highest during the first year of life. The vast majority of Followers’ children who died were infants. But nationally, fatalities in this age group tend to follow premature birth or profound congenital disorders. The deaths among Followers’ infants came from ailments that rarely take children’s lives.

articles.title: Immersive Gamebox brings controller-free gaming to new location south of Seattle this week
articles.author: Kurt Schlosser
paras: Immersive Gamebox , a global interactive group gaming company, is coming to the Seattle region with its first Pacific Northwest location opening this week at Westfield Southcenter mall.
Designed for groups of two to six players, the venue uses projection mapping, touch-sensitive walls, 3D motion tracking, and spatial audio to create controller-free, immersive gaming environments.

Players use their bodies and movements to interact directly with the room to play titles based on major media franchises, including Netflix’s “Squid Game,” “Batman,” “Angry Birds,” and “Floor Is Lava.”
A grand opening celebration on Friday starts at 10 a.m. and includes a 2 p.m. ribbon cutting and giveaways. Bookings are currently open online , with limited availability for opening weekend.

The Tukwila location marks a strategic shift for the UK-founded company, which operates roughly 20 company-owned venues across the U.S. and more than 35 worldwide. The Southcenter space is its first step into U.S. franchising, partnering with local operators to scale the experiential tech concept across North America.

Founded in 2018 by Tough Mudder co-founder Will Dean, London-based Immersive Gamebox (formerly Electric Gamebox) was acquired and recapitalized by Harlan Capital Partners in early 2025. The company uses proprietary, patented LiDAR tracking tech in its “smart rooms” and counts Index Ventures among its early venture backers.
Pricing varies by game and time. An hour of “Squid Game” for one adult costs $31.99 . Thirty minutes of “Floor Is Lava” for a child ages 3 to 11 is $23.99 .
Immersive Gamebox will be open Monday through Saturday from 10 a.m. to 9 p.m. and Sunday from 11 a.m. to 7 p.m.

articles.title: Washington state pioneered a privacy model for the nation — when will it finally pass the law at home?
articles.author: Grace Kaste
paras: More than 20 states have now passed the “Washington model” of privacy legislation. Washington state hasn’t.

In the years since then-state Sen. Reuven Carlyle introduced the Washington State Privacy Act in 2019, the blueprint has been adopted across the country, mandating that companies get the consent of consumers before collecting sensitive personal data, and providing consumers with the right to correct and delete their details in those databases.

In its home state, the bill stalled in negotiations between the House and Senate two years in a row. Every year since, a comprehensive privacy bill has been introduced in the Washington state Legislature but has failed to pass.

Washington state Attorney General Nick Brown released his office’s first data privacy report Aug. 14, calling on lawmakers to pass a privacy law that would limit how much personal information companies can collect and keep in the first place.
But that proposal will face the same hurdle that has blocked efforts to pass a state privacy law for seven years: a fight over whether consumers should be able to sue companies that violate it.

“The attorney general supports greater data privacy protections for Washingtonians,” said Mike Faulk, a spokesperson for the AG’s office. “In our experience, this has proven to be a difficult subject for the Legislature to build consensus on.”

Experts say the stakes are rising as AI systems train on personal data that often falls outside Washington’s existing privacy protections. Without a baseline privacy law, they say, lawmakers also have less to build on when they try to regulate AI itself.
AI has rendered some parts of the Washington model moot, while making others more necessary than ever, according to policy experts.
As states have begun to pass the first AI regulations, one of the highest priorities has been the regulation of AI-based high-risk decisions.

In Washington, for example, the state Legislature passed the Prior Authorization Transparency Act , which bars health insurers from using AI as the only basis to deny, delay or modify care. Washington state lawmakers also considered a bill to regulate the use of AI to make decisions of financial, educational, or legal consequence.

This is proving to be a much easier lift in states that passed the “Washington model,” often years before the current AI craze. That’s because Carlyle’s bill happened to include what’s now known as an automated decision-making technology (ADMT) opt-out clause, which granted residents the right to opt out of automated profiling when used for “legal or similarly significant effects.”
Algorithmic wage and price determinations, as well as AI-based healthcare and employment technologies, could be regulated under the pre-existing privacy act, or by tweaking those laws.

“The states that have passed automated decision making laws have done so on top of existing privacy laws,” said Cobun Zweifel-Keegan, a managing director at the International Association of Privacy Professionals (IAPP). “There’s already restrictions, or at least the beginnings of restrictions, on automated decision making baked into these privacy laws. It’s a natural model to build on top of.”

Meanwhile, AI has made it more dangerous to go without a privacy law, because an absence of privacy legislation means more personal data online for AI models to access, said Kara Williams, counsel at the Electronic Privacy Information Center .
Williams said data minimization could prevent or limit companies from repurposing personal data to train AI systems.

“It goes back to using the data for the purpose you collected it for,” Williams said. “Almost all of the data that companies have used to train AI systems or develop the algorithms that led to this moment were not collected for the purpose of training AI systems.”
Data minimization requires companies to restrict the collection and use of customer data to the service the customer requested. That often precludes secondary uses like selling it to a data broker.
The Washington attorney general’s privacy report also endorsed a data minimization standard, which the original Washington model does not include.
Carlyle said he might have written one in, if he were drafting the bill today.
“We live in an AI world with a giant vacuum in the sky, sucking up every ounce of data that exists on a person,” Carlyle said. “So I think the concept [of data minimization] makes some sense.”
Meanwhile, experts say AI makes some elements of the Washington model irrelevant.

Zweifel-Keegan of IAPP said those elements include the right to control, correct, and delete personal data, which was the bread and butter of Carlyle’s bill. Because LLMs are a weighted map of associated words, there is no straightforward way to selectively delete or change information once a model has been trained.

“That’s just fundamentally how LLMs work. They’re not a table where you can go to my name and see all the other records that are associated with me,” Zweifel-Keegan said. “You can’t go in and selectively delete information.”
While states around the country that have passed the Washington model are now seeking to revise its provisions to meet the AI moment, Washington state has no comprehensive privacy law to start with.
“AI is making us rethink some of our foundational expectations of what a privacy law does,” Zweifel-Keegan said. “Washington could be the place where that happens.”

In 2019, when now-retired State Sen. Carlyle introduced the Washington State Privacy Act, it passed the Senate 46-1 before dying in the House. One year later, it passed both chambers but died after a long and heated fight in conference.
Some say the bill didn’t deserve to pass after being “rewritten” by tech lobbyists. Others say the lawmakers who opposed the bill let the perfect be the enemy of the good.

The original bill was based on an opt-out framework, also called “notice and consent,” which required a platform to present a privacy policy to users who consent to the collection of their data by continuing to use the platform. The bill’s sole enforcement mechanism was the state attorney general, and did not offer a private right of action for individuals to sue companies that violated the proposed rules.
In 2019, Carlyle was focused on establishing a baseline notion of consumer rights — one that could be revised later, as other states ultimately did.

“At that time we didn’t have a direct understanding that consumers have a right to correct or delete their personal data, we didn’t have an understanding of what opt out meant for advertising, or an understanding of data brokers and the role that they play,” Carlyle said.
His bill also established special protections for sensitive data and frameworks to hold corporations accountable for complying with transparency and disclosure requirements.
“Those were pretty novel pillars that didn’t exist,” Carlyle said. “That’s why it had a big effect on other state laws.”
By March 2021, Virginia had passed a privacy law closely modeled off of Carlyle’s template, and over the next few years, more than 20 other states did, too.

In Washington, meanwhile, no progress was made. After Microsoft endorsed the Senate bill in 2019, consumer advocacy groups and some state lawmakers said that the tech lobby’s influence had gone too far. The state House countered with a stronger privacy bill, premised on opt-in data collection frameworks and enforced by a private right of action.

Both the 2019 and 2020 legislative sessions ended in failed negotiations between the state Senate and House over their competing privacy laws. Every year since 2021, Rep. Shelley Kloba has introduced a bill that preserves the House’s stronger language. It has yet to make it to the House floor.

The sticking point for Washington negotiators in 2019 and 2020 was the enforcement mechanism. Carlyle’s bill proposed state attorney general enforcement, while the House bill, led primarily by then-Rep. Zack Hudgins, included an additional private right of action.
Consumer advocacy groups are firm in their support for a private right of action as part of a data privacy law.

“Attorney general enforcement alone is not sufficient to enforce privacy laws, just because of limited resources and staff and funding that attorneys general across the country face,” said Williams, the EPIC counsel. “We need a stronger enforcement mechanism, like a private right of action, that would allow consumers to vindicate their own privacy rights and to take companies to court who have violated their privacy rights.”
For some in the tech industry, a private right of action is seen as unnecessarily harsh, stymieing innovation while AG enforcement would have sufficiently guaranteed compliance.

“I believe that the difference is, are you looking to get companies to comply and have clear enforcement or are you looking to punish?” said Rose Feliciano, TechNet executive director of policy for the Northwest United States. TechNet is a trade association that includes tech industry giants such as Amazon and Google.

articles.title: How the FTC’s last-minute settlement with Zillow and Redfin reshapes their $100M rentals deal
articles.author: Todd Bishop
paras: Zillow and Redfin settled an antitrust case with the Federal Trade Commission and five states Monday, just as a trial was set to begin, agreeing to undo part of a $100 million partnership that the government said effectively paid Redfin to stop competing in apartment rental advertising.

The companies, both based in Seattle, have been rivals in online real estate and related services for the better part of two decades, expanding into rentals to build their businesses beyond the market for single-family homes. The FTC alleged the deal combined two of the three largest online apartment listing services against one main competitor, CoStar’s Apartments.com.

The proposed settlement requires Redfin, now owned by Rocket Cos. , to relaunch its apartment advertising operation within six months — hiring a general manager, a sales force and a trained customer support team, while committing to spend millions of dollars to grow the business.
Redfin faces fines if it misses deadlines, and must report regularly to the FTC on its progress.

Zillow’s apartment listings will still appear on Redfin.com, Rent.com and ApartmentGuide, and Redfin will keep syndicating them, so Zillow is holding onto the audience it gained in the 2025 deal. The companies say the syndication will run through at least 2030.

What ends is the exclusive nature of the partnership: As part of the FTC settlement, Redfin is no longer barred from selling its own advertising alongside those listings, or from doing business on its own with the property managers shifted to Zillow under their original deal.

Zillow also must help Redfin rebuild. Under the order, which runs 10 years, Zillow is required to give Redfin employee information so it can recruit Zillow workers, waive any noncompete or anti-poaching agreements blocking those hires, and let apartment advertisers locked into Zillow contracts renegotiate without penalty for nine months after Redfin relaunches.
The companies will also pay the states $2 million in costs and fees, according to Washington Attorney General Nick Brown, who co-led the five-state coalition.
Zillow said the partnership “will continue unchanged,” and framed the standalone advertising products both companies plan to launch in 2027 as added flexibility for property managers.

“This resolution is a win for renters and multifamily housing providers,” said Michael Sherman, general manager and senior vice president of Zillow Rentals, in a statement. He said the partnership has brought “more leads and leases to property managers and more options to renters,” and that the standalone products will let Zillow “do even more to support the marketplace.”

The FTC offered its own take: “Today’s settlement unwinds an agreement under which Zillow paid Redfin $100 million to stop competing and hand off all its customers to Zillow,” said Daniel Guarnera, director of the FTC’s Bureau of Competition. “This kind of payment to a competitor to exit a market and stop competing violates the antitrust laws.”

FTC Chairman Andrew Ferguson called it “a complete victory for the American people” in a thread on X early Monday . He added, “This anticompetitive agreement is now history under our proposed settlement.”
Guarnera said the settlement “delivers better, quicker, more certain results” than the agency would have been able to achieve if it had gone to trial and prevailed.

“Today’s settlement will restore competition by paving the way for Redfin to re-enter the market as a stronger competitor,” Brown said in a statement. “Most importantly, consumers will have more choices and won’t be subjected to illegally manipulated prices.”

The FTC and state cases were consolidated last year. Zillow and Redfin moved to dismiss in January, and U.S. District Judge Anthony Trenga denied that motion in May, according to Real Estate News . However, the FTC’s case had met resistance in July, when Trenga denied its request to declare the deal presumptively unlawful, finding genuine disputes of material fact.
Redfin called the outcome “a significant win for Redfin and consumers across the country.”

“This agreement allows us to maintain our rental partnership with Zillow through at least 2030, while building and investing in a standalone rentals business of our own,” a spokesperson said, adding that renters “will continue to have access to the rental inventory they rely on today.”
The proposed settlement, announced Monday morning, requires court approval.
Updated with details from Washington AG Nick Brown.

articles.title: At El Cerro, high-altitude Puerto Rican coffee meets Capitol Hill cafe heights
articles.author: CHS Staff
paras: Don’t wait. It already seems nearly impossible for El Cerro to keep bringing fresh roasted Puerto Rican coffee beans to Capitol Hill.
The cafe at the top of Pike/Pine is settling in after its summer opening and has recently expanded hours. It is now serving Wednesday through Sunday 7 AM to 4 PM.

CHS reported here in July on the new E Pike cafe from Jehú Torres Vega as the entrepreneur said he was channeling his Caribbean roots in creating the new warm and inviting addition to the neighborhood’s increasingly international coffee scene.
Its name translates to, appropriately, The Hill .

The new Capitol Hill cafe is focusing on Café Alto Grande, a premium Arabica coffee cultivated in the central mountain region of Puerto Rico and known for its sweet aroma, bright profile, and smooth finish. Sourcing the special bean consistently at scale is rare and expensive compared to more standard coffees of the Americas.
El Cerro is eating some of the cost of speciality with latte prices comparable to other Hill cafes working with more standard roasts.
El Cerro would also love for you to eat some pan sobao, handing out free slices of the delicious bread in a bid to get Capitol Hill hooked.

Meanwhile, coffee lovers looking for caffeinated flavors of the Caribbean will be happy to find specialities like the cafecito, a strong, sweet Cuban-style espresso topped with a sugary cream foam on the “De La Casa” menu.
El Cerro is open at 1316 E Pike. Learn more at elcerro.net .

articles.title: The city put off sewer work until it was an emergency — Now 12th and Pike closure will double to 6 weeks
articles.author: Justin Carder
paras: A photo posted by the Unicorn last week: “Even though we’ve got some construction going on, the bar is still OPEN and we’re still having a grand ol’ time!”

An intersection’s utilities overhaul in the heart of Pike/Pine will take twice as long as originally planned after excavation crews ran into unmapped wiring, old concrete, and tangled utility lines, city officials confirmed. The even more intense punch of construction in the neighborhood is making for a challenging end of summer for residents and businesses in the area.
The round-the-clock intersection closure at E Pike and 12th Ave initially slated to last three weeks has been extended to roughly six weeks.

According to a Seattle Public Utilities spokesperson, while the project’s overall scope remains unchanged, digging beneath the street uncovered unexpected concrete, electrical wiring, and utility conflicts. The unanticipated conditions forced crews to install additional shoring to safely reach and replace 53 feet of failing, 12-inch sewer main buried 25 feet below the surface.

The intensity of the shutdown is due, of course, to the neighborhood’s aging infrastructure but is also an unfortunate byproduct of policies that put the work off for years despite obvious end of lifecycles for the old pipes and equipment below Pike/Pine.

SPU officials tell CHS that the emergency nature of the actively failing infrastructure ruled out breaking the repair into smaller, intermittent phases and staging the work in piecemeal closures would have dragged disruptions out for six to eight months and significantly elevated the risk of a catastrophic sewer failure, the utility said.

SPU owns and maintains approximately 1,400 miles of mainline sewers. Significant portions of the network date back over 100 years. As of about four years ago, roughly 40% of Seattle’s core system was vitrified clay pipe installed between the 1890s and 1940, according to city documentation.

Rather than wholesale replacement, SPU assesses pipes on a likelihood vs. consequence matrix. Pipes beneath major arterial intersections or near sensitive waterways are flagged for higher-priority intervention. Major projects like the overhaul that created the RapidRide G also provide opportunities to dig in and upgrade the system.

Adding to complications are the multiple departments involved in the work. In Seattle, street projects are managed through a multi-agency framework where the Seattle Department of Transportation acts as the regulatory gatekeeper of the city’s public right-of-way. When a project slips schedule or creates severe local impacts, the public and business owners sometimes struggle to identify who is in charge. SDOT manages the detours and permits, SPU manages the sewer, City Light handles the electrical vaults, and Puget Sound Energy manages gas lines. If a project stalls, agencies often point to other utilities’ uncompleted work or review processes.

Seattle’s historic core including Capitol Hill contains over a century of undocumented utility lines, abandoned streetcar tracks, and unrecorded concrete vaults. When one agency begins digging and encounters an unmapped line belonging to another utility, work can stall and projects quickly expand.

Another issue is staging the work. Agencies generally work sequentially rather than concurrently in the same trench for safety and liability reasons. If SCL or PSE is delayed in relocating a wire or gas pipe, SPU’s contractor must hold, pushing out the entire timeline and SDOT’s final repaving date.

With the extended timeline at 12th and Pike compounding concerns for surrounding retailers and nightlife venues, the city says it is ramping up mitigation efforts to keep local commerce afloat. Representatives stated that outreach teams are conducting door-to-door visits with business owners to resolve loading and access issues, hosting weekly virtual check-ins, and pairing with the Office of Economic Development for evening visits.

City officials emphasized that pedestrian access to all storefronts remains open, aided by new informational flyers and “Businesses are Open” signage though some property owners say they are having to foot the bill for signs for their commercial tenants.

Limited vehicle turn movements also continue under the direction of on-site traffic officers. SPU noted it is coordinating directly with fall neighborhood events, including Elysian’s Great Pumpkin Beer Festival on October 3rd to minimize impact.
The issues have been extra punishing for the nearby Unicorn bar. It suffered through a three-month closure at the end of last summer after a fire damaged the E Pike building it calls home.
“Come support your local bar, grab a drink, eat some food, and hang out with us while we ride out the construction chaos,” the bar wrote in a social media update last week.
CHS reported here in July on the $6.5 million project originally planned for a 90-day cycle of closures and construction to replace 115-year-old infrastructure in the neighborhood.

articles.title: Seattle mayor signs executive order to speed up Vision Zero including work where cyclist was hit and killed at 12th and Yesler
articles.author: CHS Staff
paras: Mayor Katie Wilson signed her executive order to accelerate Seattle’s Vision Zero initiative in an event Friday near an underway pedestrian safety construction project outside South Seattle’s Cleveland High School .

“Seattle should be a city where families can feel safe getting where they need to go — whether they’re walking their kids to school, biking to the park, or taking transit,” Wilson said in an announcement of the order. “We’ve made important progress, but every serious injury or death on our streets is one too many. We know what makes our streets safer. This Executive Order is about turning our commitment into action — getting proven safety improvements on the ground and bringing the full City together to prevent serious injuries and deaths.”

The executive order directs the Seattle Department of Transportation to fast-track high-priority safety improvements across high-crash corridors. Key measures include completing the SW Wildwood Place protected bike lane by late 2026, advancing Phase 2 of the 12th Ave S Safety Project, increasing intersection visibility through daylighting, and upgrading 19 high-collision locations along major routes like Aurora Ave N and Rainier Ave S.
The order including the emphasis on 12th Ave comes following the June tragedy at 12th and Yesler that took the life of 30-year-old Christian Salyer .

To reduce dangerous driving speeds, the directive also deploys pedestrian head-start signals at 40 intersections, adjusts signal timing, and authorizes the phased rollout of automated traffic safety cameras across up to 10 locations. The specific list of the 40 intersections and other locations were not included in the announcement.

Additionally, the order establishes a citywide interdepartmental safety team, creates a public-facing traffic safety dashboard, and targets expanding the School Streets Program to 40% of eligible schools. The city will also mandate enhanced safety features on municipal and contractor fleets while lobbying the Washington State Legislature to lower the legal blood-alcohol concentration (BAC) limit to 0.05%.

The order joins legislative efforts underway at the city council under the Seattle SAFER Streets Act , a legislative package introduced last week to update the Seattle Municipal Code to formally adopt SDOT’s Vision Zero Action Plan as the city’s official guide, requiring the Safe System Approach to guide arterial speed limits, infrastructure planning, and intersection reviews.

Seattle’s primary Vision Zero goal is to eliminate all traffic fatalities and serious injuries on city streets by 2030. In 2025, Seattle recorded 27 traffic fatalities, with pedestrian deaths — like the collision with a food delivery driver that killed Lilli Moreno as she crossed E Pine in February — representing the majority of fatal incidents across the city.

articles.title: Strauss Proposes Program Phasing Out Street Parking for RVs
articles.author: Amy Sundberg
paras: At the public safety committee meeting on August 11, Seattle Councilmember Dan Strauss introduced a legislation package that he said would help people who are currently living in their recreational vehicles (RVs). However, while the package includes funds for services such as safe lots and RV storage, it also introduces a RV permit program aimed at removing all RVs on Seattle’s streets – a move that advocates say could leave RV residents worse off.

In Seattle, people can currently park their RVs overnight in industrial areas or, according to posted signage, up to 72 hours in one place, like other vehicles. However, the new legislation would change the law so that RVs could only park for two hours in one place, and would be forbidden from parking anywhere overnight (from midnight to 6am). Failure to follow these laws could result in towing without notice.

The only exception to this new rule would be for people living in RVs and “fifth wheel” trailers who succeeded in applying for a special permit during a one-time census. In order to receive a permit, residents would have to agree to receive services and ultimately move into other housing or shelter. There would be one permit per person who would have to prove they were the registered owner of the vehicle.

In order to retain a permit, residents would have to abide by a number of regulations , including having the vehicle display a license plate and vehicle identification number, not leaving trash around, not hosting a group of five or more people, not leaving a pet tied up unattended, etc.
Permit holders would be able to turn down up to six offers of shelter or housing, but after that, they would lose their permit.
Strauss framed his plan as a way to help people who live in their vehicles.

“Today, we have zero places for people who live in their vehicles to come inside to. We have no city systems or city teams that are designed to help people that are experiencing homelessness with vehicles,” Strauss told The Urbanist . “We need to create those systems, and from there as well, RVs are a unique type of vehicle that are not built for year-round habitation.”

The legislation package consists of five ordinances and a resolution. In addition to the permitting program, the ordinances would update outdoor storage land use codes, expand the Finance and Administrative Services (FAS) Director’s authority to execute various related leases, clarify and add two new criteria to the definition of a “junk vehicle,” and allocate $5 million of funding.

The resolution states the intent to move the ecoblocks that have multiplied in industrial areas popular for RV parking, such as Ballard, SODO, and West Seattle, within six months of implementation of the program. However, it doesn’t specify who holds responsibility for ensuring this removal takes place, which can be a costly endeavor and requires somewhere else to store the heavy blocks.

The proposed funding for Strauss’s program would consist of $1.5 million in one-time dollars and $3.5 million in ongoing funds. Part of the money would be used to pay for eight new positions: seven new outreach counselor positions within the Human Services Department (HSD) and one new permit technician within the Seattle Department of Transportation (SDOT). As written, the legislation gives SDOT the task of establishing program standards and administrative procedures for the permitting program.
Alison Eisinger, the executive director of the Seattle/King County Coalition on Homelessness, questioned the plan to hire new outreach workers as part of the overall strategy.

“Seven or eight full-time city employees suggests a disproportionate investment in coordination of inadequate resources, as opposed to an investment in adding good resources that will help get more people where they need to go,” Eisinger said.

The Unified Care Team – the interdepartmental team that performs the City’s homelessness outreach and sweeps – has tallied 145 vehicles that meet the permitting program’s definition, Strauss said, adding he believes this is an undercount.

In addition to the safe lot – Glassyard Commons – opening in West Seattle in November, Strauss’s plan calls for a second safe lot. Assuming the second lot is the same size, that could mean 150 parking spaces for RVs. But Strauss said he wants to collaborate with service providers to decide whether the second safe lot should prioritize RVs.

Seattle Public Utilities (SPU) already runs an RV Wastewater Program in order to mitigate RV wastewater spill incidents, in partnership with St. Vincent de Paul. Every quarter. the team performs an average of 300-400 wastewater pump-outs.

“Before the program was launched, spill incidents peaked at 117 in 2019,” an SPU spokesperson told The Urbanist . “In its first year, the program reduced spills by 60%, and incidents have continued to decline in both frequency and severity. Today, spill incidents average about 10 per year and our estimates show the program saved about $300,000 in cleanup costs in 2025 through this proactive spill reduction work.”
Strauss was clear with The Urbanist that he ultimately wants to remove RVs from Seattle’s streets.

“We want to create a program that serves humans, that centers humans, and we're at a point where RVs are not an appropriate type of vehicle to be on our streets anymore here in our city,” Strauss said. “I think of it like a boat. You know, people have boats, and they can either park them in their driveway, which is off of a city street or they can store it, in the same way that an RV can be parked in your driveway or it can be stored.”

The analogy is an interesting one since boats are generally considered to be luxury consumer goods while unhoused people living in their RVs often have few resources and fewer choices. Houseless RV owners rarely own land on which to store their RV, hence the dilemma.
Strauss also said the permitting program would only address people living in RVs and travel trailers.

“If they are in a place in their life where they're choosing living in a vehicle, [that] is a better option than anything else, there's nothing in this legislation that outlaws, bans, or penalizes living in a vehicle. We are saying we're not going to allow RVs on the street anymore, which means somebody could live in a 15-passenger van. They could live in their truck, a truck with a camper on it,” Strauss said. “If you want to own a different type of vehicle, you have that ability.”
“The people I know who've lived in RVs, that's been the best option available. Period. It's not about choosing one RV over another or one vehicle over another,” Eisinger told The Urbanist .

Graham Pruss, the executive director of the National Vehicle Residency Coalition, used to be the only outreach worker for people living in vehicles in Seattle between 2013 and 2015, with a caseload of around 1,500 people. Pruss said people living in their vehicles saw it as a more stable option to the alternative, one that provided privacy, a place to store their belongings, and sometimes even a way to build a kind of property equity, all while maintaining a connection with their community.

“The folks that were living in vehicles often described a much deeper level of stability, a deeper level of connection,” Pruss said. “They often had bills that they had to pay, maintenance for their vehicle. They had to keep their driver's license, their insurance. They often keep it operable. At the very least, they saw this vehicle as an important piece of property.”
While advocates are pleased about the idea of more services, they are concerned at the punitive nature of the RV permitting program.

“How does this permit proposal fit into our landscape of housing and shelter? It doesn't. The permit, the way that it's currently constructed, it would be punitive and not helpful to move people into shelter or housing,” Hali Willis, the community policy manager of the Seattle/King County Coalition on Homelessness, told The Urbanist . “We like to support efforts that are based in evidence and facts and will accomplish the goals of helping people achieve stability and live well, and we don't believe that this permitting proposal will get us there.”
A similar program in San Francisco led to more than five times the number of RVs towed versus households placed into housing through their permit program.

“I think the biggest impact we would see almost immediately is you would see more people living outside and not in vehicles,” said G.B., a volunteer with Stop the Sweeps. “This doesn't solve anything.”

G.B. called out the difficulty people living in their vehicles would have trouble filling out the necessary paperwork to apply for a permit, how they might not have proof of ownership of the RV in which they’re living, and how they might be displaced from their communities in order to take a spot in a safe lot. G.B. also called out the high price the City would be paying for towing contracts to enforce the new parking laws.

“It could be very sensible to focus on the most positive and generally broadly agreed to proposals, namely a safe parking lot, the ability to understand more about people who are living in their RVs in the city of Seattle, and this idea of potentially storing people's vehicles if the fact that they don't have anywhere to park long term could be a barrier to them being able to accept shelter or housing,” Eisinger said. “But we have also told Councilmember Strauss that we believe that it is desirable and reasonable for him to defer this idea of a complex, hard to implement, bureaucratic, and expensive permitting process that is unlikely to actually improve upon people's living circumstances, and he has articulated a willingness to continue the conversation.”
Jay from Stop the Sweeps said that the services provided by the new legislative package might not be worth the punitive measures.

“It really feels like this is completely aligned with the standard thinking of the strategic approach to addressing homelessness, which is that every carrot must have a stick,” Jay said. “We can't just roll out additional services. They must be accompanied by punishment, and in this case in particular, I think that the carrot is hardly worth the stick.”

Pruss explained that for many, housing is not only unaffordable but also inaccessible, citing the difficulties faced in obtaining housing by people impacted by the criminal legal system, undocumented immigrants, young adults just aging out of the foster care system, and more.

“This is the private property, legal, valuable asset of people who are using this to survive the housing crisis that we all see around us – the lack of emergency shelters, the lack of permanent supportive housing – it simply does not exist,” Pruss said. “And to put in further regulations does not solve that problem.”
Pruss was also concerned that the legislation would move authority to SDOT, a move that he’s seen cause trouble in Californian cities like San Jose and Oakland.

“The redesignation of the vehicle from a homeless management encampment response to the Department of Transportation takes away many of the protections of homeless management responses, and it essentially says this is now an object that is designated as an obstruction that can be removed and destroyed with very little due process, almost as though it's like just a crashed vehicle on the side of the road,” Pruss said.
During the discussion of the legislation at the public safety committee earlier this month, Councilmember Bob Kettle expressed his negative opinion of people living in RVs.

“From the public safety perspective, as pretty much everybody knows, once you have five RVs together, one's going to start dealing drugs. Once you have a drug market, you have a stolen goods market,” Kettle said. “There's a clear public safety nexus.”

“I would question the research behind that,” Pruss said. “I have been to RV parking programs that are officially run. I'm the former strategic advisor on homelessness to the city of San Jose, the third largest city on the West Coast. We ran safe and supportive parking programs with well over 50 RVs in them, and that was not the case. There was never a report of anything like that, and I have never seen research that would suggest otherwise.”

According to the legislation as written, the deadline for the City to develop the RV permitting program and begin the new parking restrictions would be April 30 of next year, with enforcement beginning by July 31.

articles.title: Stranger Suggests: Your Agenda This Week, August 24–August 30
articles.author: Julianne Bell, Shannon Lubetich, Amanda Manitach, and Megan Seling
paras: (LITERATURE) I recently devoured the novel Martyr! by poet, novelist, and editor Kaveh Akbar, so when I found out that he’d chosen Hyderabad, India-based author Kavi Yaga’s debut short story collection The Vanishings for The George Garrett Fiction Prize, my interest was immediately piqued. Akbar wrote, “I love what The Vanishings makes of empty space, of the disappeared and disappearing, the once-longed-for, the self, the empty door. Kavi Yaga has a mighty ear and these propulsive stories grip you with lines that sing, leaving you big-eyed and better-made.” Each of the eight stories in The Vanishings revolves around a different person who sets out in search of something or someone missing, only to be interrupted by some kind of unusual obstacle (including a “magic fairness cream” and a “giant talking moon bird”). Yaga will discuss her work with local writer Diana Xin. ( Elliott Bay Book Company, 7–8:30 pm, free with RSVP ) JULIANNE BELL

(FILM) Considering the glut of raunchy high school sex comedies that revolved around hetero teen boys attempting to pop their cherries in the ’90s and early-aughts, it’s about time we had a horny romp about queer girls trying to get laid. In this madcap dark comedy helmed by Emma Seligman (director of the nail-biter Shiva Baby ), two hapless losers (played by Rachel Sennott and Ayo Edebiri) scheme to start a self-defense club for women in order to hook up with their cheerleader crushes (Havana Rose Liu and Kaia Gerber). Naturally, hilarity ensues. It’s Book Smart meets Fight Club with acerbic shades of Heathers . ( Northwest Film Forum, 7 pm ) JULIANNE BELL

(PERFORMANCE) Jurassic Parking Lot , which is produced by the Habit (the same folks who put on Seattle Public Theater’s hilarious and beloved holiday tradition, A Very Die Hard Christmas ), has everything you’d want from a ’90s-obsessed Jurassic Park musical spoof. There are Seinfeld references, ridiculously oversized cell phones, sexy singing and dancing raptors, and juuuuust the right amount of very, very horny Jeff Goldblum. (Warning: Prepare yourself for a Chris Pratt jump scare, too—ahhhh!) ( Seattle Public Theater, times vary, recommended for ages 14 and up ) MEGAN SELING
Book Bingo Party at Seattle Public Library

(COMMUNITY) I’ve said before that the Seattle Public Library’s annual summer Book Bingo program is my Super Bowl, so I’m thrilled about this party that brings together readers to discuss their bingo card progress a little over a week before the final deadline. Enjoy light refreshments while mingling with fellow bibliophiles, getting suggestions for your last few blank squares, and sharing your favorite reads of the summer—in case you were wondering, mine include Cassandra at the Wedding by Dorothy Baker (Suggested by an Independent Bookseller), Looking Glass Sound by Catriona Ward (Suggested by a Library Worker), and Whidbey by T Kira Madden (Unplug). ( Seattle Public Library, Central Branch, 6–7:30 pm, free with RSVP ) JULIANNE BELL

(VISUAL ART) They’re doing it again! The masterminds behind IKEA-spoof STÖR, Mary Anne Carter and Lilia Deering, are putting together another pop-up art exhibition and retail experience, Inconvenience Store. Where STÖR—in all its Swedish meatball glory—fleshed out the sprawling Base Camp 2, this new venture inhabits the ghost of a former 7-Eleven at Third and Pine, on the ground floor of the new office high-rise-turned-art-space, Parnassus. Inconvenience Store will feature artist-made renditions of familiar goods, organized by department (Food & Pantry, Beauty & Personal Care) by over 50 artists, including Colleen Louise Barry, Shiloh Davies, Emma Kates-Shaw, Maayan Haim, and more. A soft opening is planned for August 28 during the downtown art walk. ( Parnassus Project, 6–9 pm, free ) AMANDA MANITACH

(MUSIC) Writer, designer, and “Music Person” podcast host Dylan Tupper Rupert is the mastermind behind this scrappy DIY annual music festival, which takes place in the backyard of the James Beard-nominated restaurant Houlme on Orcas Island. The weekend kicks off with a welcome party on Friday night, followed by a stacked lineup on Saturday: ’90s indie rock/slowcore cult favorites Ida, Oakland alt-country-ish band Mildred, Olympia-born ensemble Gun Outfit, Minneapolis lo-fi indie project Walker Rider (“queer love songs leaning into limerence”), and LA-based “digital twang” singer-songwriter Deloyd Elze. You can expect “luxurious hot dogs,” a steady flow of wine, and a potential dip in the Salish Sea—does this not sound like the makings of a perfect summer weekend? Camping is also available by way of nearby Alder Vulture, a privately owned 10-acre property on the island. ( Houlme, Eastsound, WA, 2–11 pm, all ages ) JULIANNE BELL
Linda’s Fest: Helms Alee, Suzzallo, Filth Is Eternal, Sux, and More

(MUSIC) The poster for Linda’s Fest pretty much sums up what everyone thinks when they find out beloved dive bar and brunch spot Linda’s Tavern is once again hosting its mini music festival: “Oh fuck yes.” Though local band Linda From Work doesn’t actually have any members named Linda, I’m stoked to see their infectiously energetic garage rock/dance punk music on the bill (we love a theme). Dark Chisme, who recently blew my mind at Capitol Hill Block Party, performs a punk set instead of their typical synth-infused gothic tunes, and the Blood Brothers’ vocalist Johnny Whitney brings the cathartic art-punk of his new band Evil Island to the patio for their first Seattle show. Also on the lineup: local rock veterans Helms Alee, Rocky Votolato’s alt-rock project Suzzallo, hardcore group Filth is Eternal, and rollicking punk band Sux. The price of drinks may have changed since Linda’s opened in 1994, but admission to the fest remains free. ( Linda’s Tavern, 4 pm, 21+ ) SHANNON LUBETICH

(FILM) Filmmaker Gregg Araki’s 2004 indie classic Mysterious Skin , adapted from Scott Heim’s novel of the same name, was made over the course of three weeks on a shoestring budget. Years later, it’s finally received a painstaking 4K restoration supervised by Araki and distributed theatrically by Strand Releasing. The film follows the effects of childhood sexual abuse on two eight-year-old Little League teammates in Kansas, Neil (Joseph Gordon-Levitt) and Brian (Brady Corbet), over the years: Neil becomes a sex worker and moves to New York City, while Brian becomes obsessed with the notion that he was abducted by aliens when he was younger. Strong performances from the young leads and a haunting shoegaze soundtrack result in a devastating coming-of-age story—made all the more heartbreaking by the casting of Michelle Trachtenberg, who tragically died at 39 last year. Heim will be at Northwest Film Forum for the 7 pm screenings on Saturday and Sunday for a Q&A. ( Northwest Film Forum, 3:30 pm & 7 pm ) JULIANNE BELL

articles.title: Slog AM: ICE Agents in Washington Arrested the Wrong Man, Iran’s Rial Plummets in Value, and Can the Improved Route 8 Survive Monday’s Commute?
articles.author: Vivian McCall
paras: During an operation in Lakewood to arrest a Mexican national with a final deportation order last month, ICE agents instead detained 23-year-old Venezuelan citizen Moises Velasquez, an immigrant who had entered the United States legally but was driving the same car, a grey Volkswagen GTI, as their target. In an order granting Velasquez’s habeas corpus petition to challenge his detention, US Magistrate Judge S. Kate Vaughn said agents had demonstrated a “complete lack of procedures,” heightening the risk he would be deprived of his rights under due process, reports the Seattle Times .

Velasquez was released from the Northwest Detention Center in Tacoma last Wednesday. His attorney, Bart Klein, said ICE agents merely “saw some Hispanic guy,” decided to go after him and forced him out of the vehicle. Last year, the US Supreme Court overturned a lower court ruling and gave ICE the go ahead to stop people on the basis of appearance, language, or accent, a policy also known as racism.

During one of these traffic stops in Key West, Florida on Saturday, ICE detained the Nicaragua-born father of an immigrant soldier on the USS Abraham Lincoln, the aircraft carrier deployed to the Arabian Sea for nearly nine months with conditions and morale deteriorating so much that sailors have attempted suicide . The Department of Homeland Security said Luis Manuel Aviles entered the US illegally at an unknown date and would remain in ICE custody pending removal proceedings, NBC reports . “This is heartbreaking for me,” said his son, sailor Joshua Aviles. “I don’t know how I can mentally continue working 12+ hour days knowing that my dad is somewhere, possibly being treated like a criminal.”

The exchange rate of Iran’s rial fell to a record low 2.02 million to the U.S. dollar today as Washington prepares to issue more economic sanctions on the country. The price of basic staples has soared; rice is 60 percent higher, while beef is 150 percent more expensive. “The regime’s final refuge now lies in the self-deception of fearful nations that still believe accommodating aggression can secure a durable peace,” said US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent .

Yet Iran and Oman, countries which sit on opposite sides of the Strait of Hormuz, are reportedly close to a deal to reopen the waterway and possibly help “wind down the war in the Middle East,” the AP reports .
Weather: Sunny with a high near 76, with no chance of rain in the forecast through Friday. Go enjoy it because summer is winding down. The last 8 p.m. sunset of the year is this Wednesday .

Will the 8 still be late? The expanded red bus lane on Denny Way is a go, fulfilling Mayor Katie Wilson’s campaign promise to speed up the chronically late Route 8 bus. The bus-only lanes on Denny now extend from Seattle Center to I-5. King County Metro Transit General Manager Michelle Allison said it will save 7,200 daily passengers time. “Today is sort of like Christmas,” she said. Today will be the lane’s first big test. Drivers who don’t like change, meanwhile, are considering rocketing off the Denny Way Bridge. This would also reduce traffic congestion, at least on Howell Street. Reports the Seattle Times :

“Despite new lane markings on Boren, and signal tweaks to hasten flows on Howell, the intense competition to enter Howell Street (from First Hill, downtown and South Lake Union) produced gridlock Wednesday and Thursday, when turning cars paused in crosswalks.”

articles.title: Free Taiwan Music Festival Will Honor LGBTQ+ Rights and Promote HIV Awareness
paras: An upcoming free outdoor Taiwanese music festival comes with a mission: to celebrate LGBTQ+ visibility and promote HIV/AIDS awareness, topics that have been difficult to discuss openly in many Asian communities.

Formosound is a local music event that's partnering with the A+ Love concert series. A+ Love is a Taiwanese organization that has produced large-scale concerts featuring Mandopop (Mandarin pop music genre) icons since 2018 to uplift LGBTQ+ communities and fight the stigma of HIV/AIDS. The collaboration marks the first high-profile Mandopop-Taiwanese music festival in the U.S. Formosound will feature a performance by Taiwanese American drag queen Felicia Oh from New York City and will offer a food and vendor market with close to 50 local vendors.
Formosound takes place in Redmond's Downtown Park on Aug. 29.

"When Taiwan legalized same-sex marriage in 2019, it brought hope to young people, but there's still quite a way to go for Taiwan to be more open to LGBTQ groups," Kuo Tze (郭子) , an award-winning musical artist and co-founder of A+ Love, said through an interpreter. "In the rural areas, LGBTQ [people] are not as accepted, and there's strong resistance from the religious community."

Ohay Angah, a University of Washington doctoral student who identifies as gay and Indigenous Taiwanese from the Pangcah/Amis People, has experienced the stigma. Though she said her father can't accept her sexual orientation because of his religion, she described one benefit of legalized same-sex marriage: "Before this act passed, my mother couldn't accept same-sex marriage [or] me with a girlfriend. But after, my mother kind of accepted same-sex relationship, but had a conservative view." Angah continued, "She told me, 'Your wife will need to live with us and cook and clean the home,' just like a [Taiwanese] traditional wife." Angah said people in Taiwan are more willing to talk about this topic, but there are still cultural barriers.

The Taiwanese community has grown in the greater Seattle area to well over 10,000 people, contributing to a demand for up to 50 direct weekly flights to Taipei at peak season. Formosound Music Festival stage manager and Kent resident Harley Pan said that while many Taiwanese tech workers rent or own houses on the Eastside or live in South Lake Union, a growing number are purchasing homes in Renton, Kent, Tukwila, and Southeast Seattle.

"At Kent Station [Shopping Center] there's now a Dough Zone, and … a Taiwanese MissBoba is in downtown Kent and in Renton. The Southcenter area has Taiwanese-owned shops, including Din Tai Fung, Kizuki Ramen, Boiling Point, TP Tea, and Coco Boba, among other new Asian businesses. If you see Taiwanese food, you know that Taiwanese immigrants probably live in the area," said Pan.

Another vendor at the Formosound market will be Champion Gourmet , a Taiwanese eatery located in Kent's Great Wall Shopping Mall. It will offer dishes like Taiwanese cold noodles, braised tofu, and pig ear. "I wanted to open a restaurant that values our community," said Champion Gourmet owner Annie Lin through an interpreter. She added that she enjoys serving the community, "especially the elderly customers [who] remind me of our elders back in Taiwan."

Robin Liao, Formosound's director, has headed up the collaboration and fundraising for this event with the Taiwanese Association of Greater Seattle, the Greater Seattle Taiwanese Women's Association, and the Taiwanese Junior Chamber of Commerce in partnership with A+ Love. Liao is also a musician, having played in gothic metal and melodic death metal bands in Taiwan.

"Music is a language with no boundaries or rules," said Liao. "Music is a good vehicle to gather people to address and advocate for human rights. [People can] feel what they feel with the music [and] listen to the lyrics."

Angah said she's listened to all the featured A+ Love artists in Taiwan. She especially looks forward to seeing music artist Enno Cheng (鄭宜農) , who's a headliner in the festival. Cheng is a famous singer who came out publicly when she divorced her husband, who was another well-known singer. She's known as a dedicated and public advocate for the LGBTQ+ community through songs and writing. Angah said one of Cheng's songs reminds her that "we can gradually remove that 'not-okay' [messaging], be honest … and grow into being more authentically ourselves eventually."
