articles.title: Sound Transit Says Train Derailment Was Isolated Incident
articles.author: Doug Trumm
paras: After a snag-free stretch setting ridership records during the World Cup, Sound Transit has had a few big service hiccups in the past month and a half, with a derailment on August 1 topping the list.

A roof hatch issue on July 9 also caused a major service disruption that lasted 15 hours, after the malfunctioning hatch took out an overhead wire between the University of Washington and U District stations.

"Mechanical issues disrupted trains on July 10th and again on July 20th , when brakes on a train wouldn’t release ," Seattle Transit Blog's Sherwin Lee recounted . "Then the following day on July 21st, a power outage resulted in a temporary suspension of service between Beacon Hill and Tukwila International Blvd stations."
However, the agency has said that overall service reliability is trending up, and emphasized they have no reason to expect the derailment or roof hatch issue to repeat.

The derailment on Saturday, August 1 happened at low speed in the Chinatown-International District (CID) station just before midnight. It caused no injuries, as the train was not yet in service and empty, other than the operator.

The derailment did, however, shut down light rail service in the downtown tunnel until 2:15pm Sunday, August 2. A full restoration of service waited while Sound Transit investigated the incident. During the disruption, Sound Transit truncated service, operating a bus bridge to replace the shuttered downtown tunnel.

Because no crossover tracks exist within the downtown tunnel, any blockage or system disruption within the tunnel typically shuts the entire downtown section from SoDo to Capitol Hill. Sound Transit has raised the idea of adding crossover tracks, but the proposal remains unfunded and yet to be queued up. Such crossover tracks would allow Sound Transit more service pattern options in the tunnel, such as bypassing a particular platform or set of platforms in emergencies or maintenance situations.
Public information about what caused the derailment was scant, other than a paywalled Seattle Times article from Mike Lindblom on Sunday morning.

King County Councilmember Claudia Balducci, who serves as one of 18 members of the Sound Transit Board of Directors, brought up the issue at the Rider Experience and Operations (REO) Committee on August 6.

"On the derailment, can I just say it's been a few days: I think we should have some more information about the cause, to be honest, because a derailment is a life-threatening situation," Balducci said. "So, I'm really interested to know that we know what happened so that it's not going to happen with a train with people on it. That's very concerning."

At Balducci's prodding, Sound Transit CEO Dow Constantine expanded on the brief summary of the derailment in his CEO report to start the meeting, which treated the incident as handled and in the rearview mirror.

"This is a section of the track that veers off and goes into a pocket track," Constantine said. "So, that is a track that is not for passengers between the north and south tracks in the International District Station. As this non-passenger train was being repositioned from the south end in order to add capacity there."
Sound Transit had been storing extra trains at the station to help handle traffic leaving the Ed Sheeran concert at Lumen Field.

"[The train] was taken onto that side track, and this is where we know the two bolts sheared off bolts that were holding that curved track that goes to the pocket track. We don't know why they sheared off, however, and so Ed [Cobean], could you talk a little bit about the investigation that's being done on those two bolts, and then on the other fasteners that are similar, and there are few of them in the rest of the system."
Ed Cobean, Sound Transit's Deputy CEO, Chief Transit Operations, pointed to steps the agency was taking to prevent another derailment on pocket tracks.

"There is only one other switch in our system – this is special track work – that has anything that resembles it." Cobean said. "So, we've already done a full inspection on the other switch. Have put the existing switch bolts back into place. It's been repaired. We are also sending those bolts out for metallurgy testing to see if they can come back to us [with improvements]. We do know that it was the original construction, original bolts from when that was built 20 years ago, and we are going to do additional testing and inspections across the entire system for other switches, not just these two alone."

The Urbanist reached out to Sound Transit this week to see how the investigation was progressing into how the bolts were sheared off without the agency's track inspection team noticing, but no new details were offered.

"We have confirmed that the shearing of the two bolts caused the track to become misaligned, resulting in the derailment," Sound Transit spokesperson Henry Bendon said in an email. "The incident occurred on a section of special track work that is unique in our system to access the pocket track at International District/Chinatown Station - although it is used in many other systems. That track was inspected, repaired, and returned to service the next day, and we have no reason to believe this will happen again."

At the REO Committee, Balducci did bring up that rider communication could have been better during the unexpected outage, noting many had reached out to her to share their confusion when the downtown tunnel closed unexpectedly.

"I just wanted to share that I personally got a whole bunch of feedback about wayfinding in the aftermath of a major unplanned disruption like that," Balducci said. "People not knowing how to get to the shuttles, and so I would love to hear some more here today, if possible, about what happened and sort of how we can upgrade our standards for making sure we have immediate announcements of delays, how long they're going to be, if we know what the cause is, and then how to get to a shuttle easily."
Constantine did acknowledge some room for improvement on that front.

"We are quite rigorous in our processing of lessons learned," Constantine said. "And we are continuing to build the agency's capacity for continuous improvement, so that each time we have something that arises that's unusual, we can learn from it, and we can make the experience better for our passengers. And this is certainly one of those events where we have opportunities to learn more and improve."
Derailments are very rare in Sound Transit's system. Lindblom reported the incident earlier this month was only the second known derailment that disrupted passenger trips since service began in 2009.

Another incident on August 10 in Rainier Beach was initially reported on social media as a derailment, but turned out to be a track switch issue that did not result in a derailment. The issue led to a comparatively short service disruption while the switch was investigated.

Sound Transit does periodically run staff through simulations to prepare them for emergency situations, including derailments. Andrea Trepadean, Chief Safety Officer at Sound Transit, described such training exercises at a REO Committee meeting in December.

"We do emergency preparedness drills and exercises, and part of those drills and exercises we do simulate self evacuation of passengers," Trepadean said at the time. "When we have those drills and exercise and there is a self evacuation, what we're focused on is the communication and the recovery of the scene and the safety of the passengers. Referencing the event on Sunday where the Sounder passengers self evacuated, the safety of the passengers was the conductor's focus. The conductor immediately pivoted to protect those passengers by making sure we had all train traffic stopped and the tracks were protected with a track block, and we had personnel activated responding to assist with a large-scale self evacuation of passengers."
Sound Transit simulated a derailment as part of preparation to launch the Federal Way Link Extension in December.

"We recently did an exercise on our Federal Way Link Extension," Trepadean said in December. "It was a full-scale exercise that we performed on October 25 and this was part of that simulation. The first responders involved in that exercise knew the general theme of the exercise, which was a simulated train derailment."

Of course, running a simulation or two does not always mean that the agency's entire apparatus is ready to seamlessly pick up the slack when a derailment happens... say near midnight on Saturday with droves of Ed Sheeran fans emptying out of a stadium to find the light rail station is suddenly shut down.

One theory for the spate of outages is that the agency was pushing the system so hard (including temporarily suspending its monthly maintenance program to squeeze out more capacity) during a ridership-heavy month buoyed by the local World Cup matches that maintenance issues piled up. According to the agency, World Cup traffic wear and tear did not relate to any of the recent service disruptions.
A draft agency service plan does look at expanding maintenance windows across the light rail network by shortening service spans at certain times.

"To your questions about maintenance windows, we are currently in the early stages of developing the 2027 service plan, and are seeking public feedback on the possibility of additional time for maintenance," Bendon said. "This would build on the success we’ve been seeing with our monthly maintenance program, but is entirely unrelated to your question about World Cup ridership."

articles.title: Wilson expedites safety projects and prioritizes Vision Zero across departments
articles.author: Michael Smith
paras: Outside Cleveland High School on Friday, Mayor Wilson unveiled her Vision Zero Executive Order . This long-awaited executive order re-prioritizes Vision Zero for the Seattle Department of Transportation (SDOT) and for other city agencies. In 2015, Seattle committed to reaching zero serious injuries or fatalities on the city’s roadways by 2030. In the decade since, 280 people have been killed and 31,000 people have been injured while traveling around Seattle. The executive order has five sections with specific deliverables from various city agencies.

Section 1 focuses on speeding up the implementation of road safety projects. Far too often, safety projects are bundled with street repaving or other infrastructure upgrades that take years to design and complete. Rather than wait on those changes, this section directs SDOT to implement safety improvements earlier while the larger projects are designed. This could include lane configurations or parking on arterial streets. In addition, this executive order directs SDOT to deliver following projects earlier than scheduled:

Section 1 also calls on SDOT to determine ways to accelerate project delivery for different project types, such as expediting community engagement, streamlining project scopes, and improving coordination with Seattle City Light (SCL) and Seattle Public Utilities (SPU). SDOT is also directed to implement intersection daylighting at any intersection that receives other improvements (similar to the No Turn on Red rollout process). Finally, Section 1 calls for an analysis of arterial road lighting conditions to identify areas that need lighting upgrades.

Section 2 focuses on improving city-owned vehicles to include protections for other road users. The Department of Finance and Administrative Services (FAS) is tasked with developing a plan to retrofit city vehicles with enhanced safety features or replace vehicles with smaller, lighter weight options. In addition, FAS will need to deliver a report that outlines the impacts of requiring all City-contracted vendors’ and sub-vendors’ large vehicles to be equipped with convex mirrors, cross-over mirrors, blind-spot awareness decals, side guards, vulnerable road user detection, automatic emergency braking, and Intelligent Speed Assistance.

Section 3 calls on SDOT and the Seattle Police Department to rollout speed cameras at ten locations around Seattle by March 31, 2029. SDOT is also tasked with identifying roads where signal timings can be adjusted to reduce vehicle speeds or increase pedestrian crossing times.

Reducing traffic injuries and deaths requires coordination from several city agencies. Section 4 of the executive order tasks SDOT with creating an interdepartmental team that will meet monthly on Vision Zero progress. This team will include representatives from SDOT, SPD, SFD, SCL, SPU, the City Attorney’s office, City Budget Office, and the Mayor’s Office. This section also calls on the expansion of the School Streets program to include 40% of eligible public schools.

The fifth and final section of Wilson’s executive order sets the priorities for the Office of Intergovernmental Relations (OIR) on a few key issues: reducing liability following street improvement projects, increasing dollar value limits on City crew projects, legislative best practices around Vision Zero, supporting local control on No Right on Red policies, supporting efforts to lower the blood-alcohol content limit to 0.05%, and increasing the maximum weight of certain vehicles subject to transportation benefit district vehicle fees.

The changes outlined in this executive order will expedite the City’s efforts to reach Vision Zero by 2030. This strong initiative has largely been missing from political leaders for the past decade. SDOT has implemented a few city-wide policies as part of the effort to achieve Vision Zero. In 2019, leading pedestrian intervals became the default option for all new or updated traffic signals. The following year, the City reduced the speed limit on almost all arterial roads to 25mph. Since 2023, No Turn on Red signs have been added to hundreds of intersections and will be applied to all new or modified intersections. This policies have seen positive results, but are not sufficient to reach zero serious injuries and fatalities by 2030. With the addition of Mayor Wilson’s policies introduced yesterday, Seattle may be able to reach its goal in the next four years.

articles.title: King County Council Sets Aside Emergency Motion to Restore Route 372
articles.author: Ryan Packer
paras: The King County Council ultimately did not consider an emergency ordinance put forward this week to retain King County Metro's Route 372 between the University of Washington and Bothell, a move made in response to rider concerns around degraded transit service if the route is retired as planned next Saturday. The ordinance, put forward by Councilmember Rod Dembowski, will instead be sent to committee for additional deliberation.

Advancing legislation directing changes to a specific bus route just 11 days before Metro's major fall service change was an extraordinary step for Dembowski to take, unprecedented in recent memory. If the ordinance had been adopted as written, it likely would have forced the state's largest transit agency to upend plans that had been in place for months, diverting operators from new routes that are planned to be launched in Northeast Seattle on August 29 back to 372 service – a very long and expensive route for Metro to operate.

Dembowski was responding to calls for a rethinking of the 372's retirement that have come from a broad array of groups, including the city councils in Bothell, Kenmore, and Lake Forest Park. The 372 is a highly used route, but most of the ridership occurs south of Lake Forest Park's city boundary at NE 145th Street, with riders in Lake City able to use the new Route 72 and 77 to access more destinations than they could previously.

The new routes comes at the cost of losing a one-seat-ride directly to the heart of the UW campus from Lake Forest Park, Kenmore and Bothell. In addition, issues have been raised about the loss of bus frequencies along Bothell Way north of NE 145th Street, and the transfer environment for riders changing buses at that specific intersection.

Anyone trying to switch between the new Metro Route 72 and Sound Transit's 522 – now set to terminate at the Shoreline South light rail station rather than Roosevelt – will have to cross the wide and dangerous state highway, or add time to their trip by transferring at the light rail station itself.

"I've done a lot of service changes, and when you eliminate a route, it's usually not very popular. People don't like to see their routes go away, and sometimes it's hard to see the replacement routes. But this one has caused quite a bit of challenges," Dembowski said in explaining the ordinance's impetus Tuesday. "I thought perhaps there might be, given the great interest in the route, a pause, an administrative pause, and they might need a legislative companion to endorse that."
A spokesperson for King County Metro told The Urbanist that an administrative pause was not planned.

"Metro is moving forward with the planned route changes on Aug. 29. We are focused on helping riders and communities navigate the new changes including with updated customer information, rider alerts, street teams, and customer information sessions," Metro's Jeff Switzer said. "There is no lost coverage as new routes replace Route 372, and there will be more service provided where the majority of ridership on the current Route 372 occurs."

Switzer provided screenshots of a travel time estimate provided by Google Maps, showing that a trip from UW Bothell to Stevens Way on the UW Seattle campus would actually be quicker with the new routing of the 522, going from around an hour exactly to 56 minutes.
Ultimately, Dembowski's ordinance looked to be more of a symbolic move than a real proposal.

"I'm not asking for a vote here today because it's not practical the way we run routes. You know, routes are picked by our drivers. You've got to have the equipment to run it. There's a lot that goes into a service change, but I did want to take a few moments to just acknowledge that this is a difficult change for the community," Dembowski said.

Direct interventions by county councilmembers into routing decisions at Metro used to be much more common, but in recent years the council has largely deferred to the agency's planners, making decisions based on a set of adopted service guidelines. That technocratic shift cuts both ways. Some councilmembers have appeared frustrated when Metro officials point to the fact that route restructures are council-approved as a reason why their options to mitigate negative impacts are limited.

"Changes to the 372 and associated routes went through years of community engagement, and the project’s Mobility Board - a group of residents who live, work, or travel in the project area – twice evaluated this route change at different phases of the planning and engagement process, selecting both times to replace Route 372 by creating the new 72 and combined service provided by Sound Transit Route 522/Stride, in order to use available public transit resources to address priority needs in these communities," Switzer said.

Riders in Lake Forest Park and Kenmore aren't the only ones that are set to see less transit service than they currently do after this month's restructure. On the Eastside, the problem may actually be more acute, with several areas no longer included in Metro's fixed route network in the wake of the full East Link Connections project, the second phase of which goes into effect next Saturday.

Hours before Dembowski's ordinance had been queued up, the county council's transportation committee discussed the receipt of a new report outlining the gaps created by that restructure, which reoriented bus service around new light rail stations in Mercer Island, Bellevue, and Redmond. The report, requested by Claudia Balducci via the county budget and delivered in April, ultimately confirmed that riders in the Woodridge, Crossroads, and BelRed areas of Bellevue have been shortchanged by the bus routing changes.
Next week, riders around Eastgate who are able to catch buses to Downtown Bellevue or Eastgate Park and Ride will also be included in that list with the elimination of the Route 271.

"What [East Link Connections] ultimately did [...] is dramatically improved frequencies around and to the light rail in certain corridors, increased service geography. It spread out service to new areas that hadn't received service before. But what we also did was we unintentionally created several new transit deserts, mostly in East Bellevue, which is one of the highest equity score areas in all of East King County, and that can't be what this was about," Balducci said this week. "This was about the introduction of major new transit service and how we were going to make that work best for the riders in that area."

The common thread between Lake Forest Park and Bellevue is a transit agency dealing with resource constraints when designing route restructures. This can cause a negative feedback loop where Metro isn't able to fully provide transit access or proper frequencies, depressing ridership and leading to decisions to reallocate service elsewhere.

While the pending network changes will add frequency and create new direct connections that will help countless riders access their destinations, the gaps that are being created also deserves attention – but probably not in the form of an ordinance blowing up a network restructure a week-and-a-half before it's set to be implemented.

articles.title: Seattle Seeks to Broaden Climate Action Plan, with Adaptation in Mind
articles.author: Syris Valentine
paras: Note: This article is part three in a three-part series on Seattle’s Climate Action Plan. Read part one on the history of climate action in Seattle here and part two on the process of updating the climate action plan here .

University of Washington’s wǝɫǝbʔaltxʷ Intellectual House bustled on July 15 during Pacific Northwest Climate Week as more than 100 local academics, philanthropists, climate professionals, environmental leaders, and staff from City departments and other surrounding agencies gathered for the Seattle Regional Partners Forum . The Office of Sustainability and Environment convened the event for an afternoon discussion about the city’s ongoing update to its climate action plan.
“Our goal in updating the climate action plan,” the project’s manager Narita Ghumman told attendees, “is to create a plan that reflects today’s challenges and prepares us for the future.”

In doing so, the developing plan is shaping up to build on the previous plan, adding a focus on resilience and cross-governmental collaboration. If Seattle is to fulfill the climate goals cemented in its 2013 plan, emissions must plunge to 58% by the end of the decade — just three and half years away. The new climate plan is seeking to invigorate more momentum on emissions at the same time it fills other, urgent gaps.

Susan Dickerson-Lange, director of UW’s climate impacts group, and Stefan Wheat, director of the planetary health program in UW’s School of Medicine, broke down the present impacts of climate change and what they mean for people’s health and wellbeing today and into the future.
“We’re moving out of the world of projections of what the future looks like,” said Dickerson-Lange.

Many people are experiencing those changes in their daily lives. Yearly temperatures are two degrees warmer across the Pacific Northwest than a century ago, she said, and average August highs have risen four degrees in the same period, elevating the risk of heatwaves and the hazards they bring, especially for a region that lacks widespread air conditioning .

These temperature changes have diminished snowfall throughout the state’s mountains and caused the snowpack that does form to melt earlier, which is changing how the region’s rivers flow — even causing some to run dry in late summer — with implications for both agriculture and ecosystem health. The recurrent droughts across the state in recent years have also made our landscapes and cities susceptible to wildfires of increasing severity and intensity.

“The key takeaway message here,” said Dickerson-Lange, “is that we are experiencing these impacts right now, and that continued action is needed to reduce harm to people, to ecosystems, and to infrastructure.”

Washington state was recently reminded of this lesson due to wildfires in Spokane and the winds that lofted the ashy remnants of several Spokane neighborhoods to mix in the atmosphere with soot from flame-engulfed forests in Oregon, British Columbia, and Central Washington to spread a blanket of smoke across the region in early August.

With 154,000 deaths around the world attributable to wildfire smoke every year, “this is not a 2050 problem,” added Wheat, a practicing physician. “This is a right now problem, and it’s showing up in emergency departments like mine.”

But the deaths and adverse effects associated with smoke and heat and other climate impacts aren’t shared evenly across a city like Seattle, he said. “There is a clear pattern: Age, chronic illness, outdoor work, housing insecurity, and race compound climate risk in overlapping and often reinforcing ways.”

For these reasons, both Wheat and Dickerson-Lange emphasized how crucial it is that Seattle seeks to build its resilience to climate change at the same time it aims to stem the tide of the forces driving the crisis forward. “Investing in adaptation is not conceding defeat,” said Wheat. “It’s a recognition of our responsibility to protect people from the harms that are already happening, and from the harms that, frankly, are already locked in no matter what we do on emissions today.”

After Ghumman, Wheat, Dickerson-Lange, and others concluded their remarks, the forum dispersed into breakout groups. Each group discussed two out of 10 “families” of possible climate actions that thematically capture the priorities the city will likely pursue through the plan. These included health, buildings, transportation, waste, water, food, energy, community preparedness, and more.

“In the action families, I was happy to see some of the actions actually resonated intimately with the recommendations [of community members],” Faduma Fido, a leader with People’s Economy Lab, told The Urbanist after the forum. Fido has provided technical assistance to the groups hosting the community assemblies that were funded by OSE and the city’s Green New Deal Oversight Board.
The category-based approach appealed to many of the attendees.

“I was really interested, seeing how they’ve taken a new approach with the action families,” Shemona Moreno, executive director of 350 Seattle, told The Urbanist . “It really is that broad. There are 10 areas [of action], and you could probably add 10 more.”

Even though 350 Seattle has long been focused on addressing the root causes of the climate crisis, Moreno had resilience and adaptation front-of-mind coming out of the forum, in part because she has seen how chronic illness has made people within 350 Seattle particularly vulnerable to heat.

Even in discussions of action families not explicitly about adaptation, participants proposed ideas that would address the topic. For instance, in a group discussing how Seattle can maintain and bolster its supply of reliable clean energy, multiple people proposed ideas that would strengthen the grid and local resilience at the same time. One suggested helping neighborhood groups to get solar power stations in case of blackouts; similarly another proposed providing community centers with battery backups. Others proposed things like community solar, balcony solar, battery installations, and other kinds of distributed energy resources that support moving toward a decentralized grid that would likely be well situated to withstand the strains of extreme weather .

Another recurrent theme was the need for the city to find ways to partner with surrounding agencies and municipalities. For instance, on the topic of food systems, one participant highlighted the need to recognize that most of the food that Seattleites eat is grown outside city limits but nonetheless remains relevant to the city’s broader climate goals, and the city must find ways to encourage both eating habits and farming practices that are planet-friendly.

Consumption-based climate pollution is something that OSE, Seattle Public Utilities, and King County have been studying, as well. In 2023, the city released a “ consumption-based emissions inventory ” that accounts for climate pollution produced directly within city limits as well as any and all emissions associated with a Seattleite’s activities, whether that be buying a car, grabbing groceries, or ordering off Amazon.

“A consumption-based emissions inventory opens up the scope a little bit more to see what else is happening in specific sectors,” Ani Krishnan, OSE’s climate data and policy manager, told The Urbanist . “So for buildings, it shifts the conversation from operational emissions to thinking about the energy and emissions expended to put that building there.”

Such inventories also would account for emissions and waste from demolitions as well. This then forces the city to think not just about incentivizing heat pumps and other electric appliances but also promoting green construction practices, like shifting from concrete to cross-laminated timber, or even second-hand building materials salvaged through deconstruction .

This consumption-based approach inherently requires the City to expand its approach to action beyond its city limits, and with King County , Puget Sound Clean Air Agency , and the Washington State Department of Ecology all having adopted their own climate action plans within the last year, the time is ripe for fostering regional partnerships.

Any collaborations should not just be about infrastructure resilience and emissions reductions, but also stewardship of the environment and crucial watersheds. “Wind blows. Water flows,” Emily Pinckney, co-founder of the nonprofit Breaking Barriers Collaborative, told The Urbanist .
Sean Dixon, executive director of the nonprofit Puget Soundkeeper, also emphasized the importance of a regional approach to water stewardship.

“We keep deciding how we govern the built environment based on artificial lines on a map drawn a century ago, as opposed to the way things work in the real world, which is watershed by watershed and microclimate by microclimate,” Dixon told The Urbanist . “If you’re not planning by the watershed, then you’re not accomplishing your goals of protecting this receiving water or protecting this community.”
This kind of approach matters across the country, he added, “and here it’s even more required because of the geology of our basin, thanks to the glaciers and how our systems work.”

As someone with a long career working to clean up and defend waterways and water bodies in Seattle and elsewhere — including in New York during the response to Hurricane Sandy — Dixon regularly thinks about climate resilience, particularly for the Duwamish Valley. The valley has already had to cope with tidal flooding , but as sea levels rise, it will only get worse. South Park and Georgetown need to be meaningfully prepared for this, he said. To Dixon, the sandbags and pumpstations that SPU has so far deployed are “literally the opposite of resilience. That is just another thing that can fail.”

As he and Puget Soundkeeper see it, meaningful solutions would involve investing in nature-based efforts that slow the flow of rainwater, threading it into the ground, and restore portions of the marshlands that were filled in across the river valley. This would in turn create bulwarks and diversions against the floodwaters.

But whether in the Duwamish Valley or elsewhere, it is becoming increasingly clear that fostering resilience to climate extremes is critical — as is eliminating emissions. So the challenge going forward for climate-concerned community groups, for the city, for the county, and for the state is to mitigate the drivers of climate change at the same time that they adapt to its dangers.
“Climate catastrophe is here,” Pinckney said, “and we have to prepare for it.”

articles.title: Wilson Order Tees Up Sweeping Traffic Safety Changes, Accelerating Projects
articles.author: Ryan Packer
paras: A beefy executive order released by Seattle Mayor Katie Wilson Friday gives marching orders to an array of City departments on the issue of traffic safety, including clear direction accelerating work on safety-oriented road overhauls at the Seattle Department of Transportation (SDOT). The document is Wilson's most ambitious transportation-oriented move to date, eight months into her term in public office – after more than a decade of work as an organizer with deep ties within the transportation advocacy community.

"The simple truth is that, despite having a Vision Zero commitment on the books for over a decade, Seattle has not met our goals on transportation safety," Wilson said Friday. "We are not on track to eliminate serious injuries and fatalities by 2030, and we still see too many headlines, too many ghost bikes, too many families in mourning. We know the tools that can make a difference: safer street designs, safer speeds, better crossings, and better visibility."

The wide-reaching order includes five different sections, giving SDOT a laundry list of specific projects to implement at the same time that the department completes an update to its Vision Zero Action Plan and provides recommendations to the mayor on how to deliver safety projects more quickly across the board.

It calls for work to upgrade the vehicle fleets used both by City employees and by city contractors to improve safety, make adjustments to Seattle City Light-controlled street lighting systems, and increase the participation rate in the school street program at Seattle Public Schools to 40%.

"SDOT's team has done outstanding work, and we have the data showing its impact on particular routes or intersections,' Wilson said. "But we have not achieved our goals yet because one department can't keep up with the scale of this challenge, and we have lacked the political will to do what works. This is what this executive order does: It directs the city to take this issue seriously, from how we design our roads to how we manage our fleet of vehicles to how we do enforcement. A key part of this order is accelerating existing safety projects, taking work already underway and helping it move forward faster."

The order drops the day after Wilson helped put final touches on a bus lane on Denny Way set to open this weekend, joined by Councilmember Alexis Mercedes Rinck and "Fix the L8" advocates who pushed for the change.

By next summer, SDOT will add intersection "daylighting" at 20 intersections, creating a clear zone intended to improve visibility close to marked and unmarked pedestrian crosswalks. Even more significantly, daylighting will be implemented over the course of routine capital maintenance, matching a similar move made around no-right-on-red signage in 2023 .

SDOT will scale up its automated traffic enforcement camera program, starting with four new locations for cameras and scaling up to 10 by spring of 2029, giving the City time to make staffing changes at the Seattle Police Department when it comes to personnel assigned to review camera violations. The department will also explore how to adjust signal timing to improve safety, a move that is a step away from projects that have sought to increase vehicle speeds with signal upgrades.

"I think what this represents is first of all, her commitment to Vision Zero, and her commitment to making sure that her action on this is substantive, impactful, and meaningful," Alex Hudson, Wilson's senior policy advisor on transportation and livability, told The Urbanist . "It is an expression of her understanding that it's a shared responsibility. Obviously, the Department of Transportation has an important role, but is not by a long shot the only department who has a role in this key public safety issue."

Councilmember Eddie Lin said his District 2 has long borne the brunt of the safety crisis, as a hot spot for fatal crashes. Addressing that is a crucial part of making the city safer. [image or embed]

Councilmembers Alexis Mercedes Rinck and Eddie Lin spoke at Mayor Wilson's press event at Cleveland High School in Beacon Hill. Lin echoed the mayor's points about the need for political will and treating traffic safety as a key part of ensuring public safety broadly. Lin's District 2 has borne the brunt of traffic violence and gun violence crises.

"Certainly, it is important for us to focus on all types of public safety,' Lin said. "You know, youth gun violence has been devastating, again for South Seattle in particular, but for some reason we talk about transit traffic safety differently. We too often see it as just part of everyday life, as if it's not something that we have the ability to change or control. And I think that's why, for too long, it has been normalized, and it has allowed us to to not take the urgent action we need to to take."

Not present at Wilson's press conference was Councilmember Rob Saka, who chairs the transportation committee. PubliCola 's Erica Barnett reported Saka was invited , but declined to attend, instead rolling out his own " Safer Street Act " as unfinished informational items on Thursday, a package which Barnett described as "mostly nonsubstantive" and a "hasty attempt to upstage her."
Two different reporters asked Wilson why Saka wasn't at the press conference, and she quickly pivoted to a collaborative note.

"I'm excited to have the partnership of our council and of the transportation chair," Wilson said Friday. "I think anyone who wants to work together to make our streets safer for all users, we're going to work together, and I'm excited about his leadership, too."

With this order, SDOT is directed to add a "new, early delivery phase" to major corridor projects in development including Rainier Avenue S , Aurora Avenue N , S Jackson Street, 4th Avenue S, and MLK Jr Way S. "These changes can impact lane configuration, turning, and parking on Seattle arterials, but SDOT should prioritize safety-first solutions tailored to the type and severity of crashes on the corridor," the order states.

These corridor overhauls are likely to be the most impactful projects in the 2024 Seattle Transportation Levy, giving the city an opportunity to redesign some of the city's most dangerous streets. But to date, few details have been made public around future street designs, as fatal and serious injury crashes continue to happen on those streets.

Other "key Vision Zero projects" are also on the list to be accelerated, including a planned protected bike lane along SW Wildwood Place and safety upgrades along 12th Avenue S – both locations of recent fatal crashes. The Mayor's Office is eying 19 other high-collision locations for changes by next fall. Francisca Stefan, SDOT's Senior Deputy Director, told The Urbanist this week that most of the projects on the list have already been in planning, with this order giving them even more urgency than they had before.

"They're all a little different, but what is largely going to be the case is they're going to jump the line, and basically, we are already doing a lot of that, but it's sort of just amplifying and and shining a stronger light on moving those things, putting them at the first of everybody's queue, and continuing to push them internally to be the first things that are out the door," Stefan said.

Longer-term, a report due next January asks for a "set of project types and criteria where adjustments to current practice could accelerate project delivery," getting safety upgrades completed more quickly. That includes exploring how to make safety adjustments separate from planned utility work, a coupling that often leads to long lead times on projects as SDOT coordinates with City Light and Seattle Public Utilities. The report also asks for recommendations on "expediting community engagement processes," a potential signal that city officials are looking to find ways to interrupt the Seattle Process when safety is at stake.

"One of the exciting things about the executive order is the forward momentum," Stefan said. "It's opening up new methods and new ways of doing things. It's exciting to see that as part of the bouquet of different efforts that we're all taking as a team."

Wilson's order also includes an entire section on safer vehicles, directing the city's department of Finance and Administrative Services (FAS) to develop a fleet transition plan intended to adjust vehicles with "safety protections for vulnerable road users by identifying opportunities to right-size fleet vehicles for smaller size, decreased weight, and reduced blind zones."

Specific safety upgrades including visibility cameras, convex mirrors, cross-over mirrors, side guards, and blind-spot awareness decals are all specifically called out in the order, which will impact new City vehicles and existing ones.

The order also includes a section on vehicles used by contractors, directing the City to explore adding some of those same features to required safety infrastructure that contractors are required to adhere to when operating under City contracts. That section even includes the potential use of Intelligent Speed Assistance (ISA) to ensure that city contractors maintain safe speeds on city streets, a provision that would likely need to be negotiated with labor unions if implemented on the city's own fleet.

"We want to make sure that we're prioritizing safe vehicles, and so that means right-sizing them," Hudson said. "We don't need to wait to purchase new vehicles to make some of these safety improvements. So we're also directing further work on retrofitting. Some of that work is already underway, and I want to give a lot of credit to the Department of Transportation and others for having made progress on this work already."

Seattle's official legislative agenda for 2026 , adopted in the final days of former Mayor Bruce Harrell's term, doesn't include any mention of traffic safety. But this order gives the City a substantive list of potential changes that the state legislature could implement to make a difference on the issue of reducing serious injuries and deaths on Seattle's roadways.

Some of those changes impact SDOT's ability to deliver projects. If the department makes immediate changes to a street following a devastating crash, the City is often found liable for that under a legal doctrine known as subsequent remedial action. Wilson's order asks the city's Office of Intergovernmental Relations (OIR) to advocate for reforms that would keep the City from being held liable from acting quickly in the wake of a crash.

The City will also push the legislature to raise the limit on capital projects that must go out to bid, a provision of state law that prevents the department from delivering modestly-sized projects with the City's own crews.

"We're doing a lot of research about this right now. Sometimes [it makes projects] up to six months longer and a minimum of 30% more expensive. So not an effective or efficient use of taxpayer dollars there, and we want to increase the threshold and index it to inflation," Hudson said.

The legislative agenda also includes a request to amend state law to allow Seattle to implement no-turn-on-red restrictions citywide without having to install a sign at every single intersection. It also references support for the statewide push for a lower, 0.05% blood-alcohol content (BAC) threshold when it comes to drunk driving, a push that has stalled out over multiple legislative sessions.

Speaking at the mayor's rollout, Gordon Padelford, executive director of Seattle Streets Alliance , mentioned the broader headwinds that make achieving zero road deaths challenging for any city, from the supersizing of SUVs and trucks to rampant speeding and distracted driving.

"I was there at the press conference in 2015 in Lake City when Vision Zero was announced as a bold new direction for the city," Padelford said. "And since then, across the United States, speeding has been rampant, distracted driving is increasing, intoxicated driving remains stubbornly high, and the proliferation of SUVs and passenger trucks that are too large for our streets is having deadly consequences, especially for pedestrians."
Padelford noted Seattle has been able to buck these negative trends to some extent, but not enough to save hundreds of people from facing severe consequences from crashes every year.

"But in the face of these headwinds, Seattle's safer than many of our peer cities: San Francisco, Minneapolis, Washington D.C., Philadelphia, Portland, and Denver. And that's a laudable achievement. We should take a moment to recognize, and it's thanks to the Vision Zero program's efforts to set safer speed limits, implement traffic calming, and build safer crosswalks," Padelford said. "But we must do more. In 2025, more than 200 Seattleites suffered life-altering injuries, and 27 lost their lives."
Several speakers brought up that behind each statistic was a human tragedy that shouldn't be sanitized as a mere numerical datapoint.

"These are not statistics; these are not numbers," Padelford said. "These are families. These are individuals with communities and friends and colleagues, and the ripples of devastation that happen from each of those incidents affects people for a long, long time, and there are stories behind each of those. And I would implore the media today to humanize the people behind the statistics to think about why they're not able to get home to their loved ones and what we can do to make sure everyone gets home safely."

Traffic safety issues consistently rank among the top public safety concerns voiced by Seattleites, with the 2025 Seattle University-conducted Seattle Public Safety Survey of nearly 9,000 residents finding that no other issue ranked higher.

"This isn't about paint on pavement for its own sake," Rinck said Friday. "It's about a mother living off of Aurora Avenue, not squeezing her child's hand a little tighter every time they cross the street. It's about an elder in the Rainier Valley being able to get to the bus stop without playing chicken with many lanes of traffic, and it's about saying finally out loud with the force of city government behind it, your life is worth more than someone else's convenience."

Friday's order has reportedly been in the works for months, gaining extra urgency following the death of Christian Salyer at 12th Avenue and Yesler Way in June and the death of Maridee BonaDea on SW Wildwood Place just a few weeks later. In its breadth, it likely represents the biggest reaffirmation of Seattle's 2015 Vision Zero commitment to eliminate deaths and serious injuries on the city's roadways by 2030 – a tall order, but certainly not one that the city will be able to make progress on without accelerating work and doubling down on safety interventions that are known to be effective.
Doug Trumm contributed to this reporting.

articles.title: Oregon Is Spending More Than Ever on Low-Income Housing. A State Law Keeps the Details Secret.
articles.author: Rob Davis
paras: Oregon’s spending on low-income housing has exploded in the past five years. The state has given developers an unprecedented $1.4 billion, and the cost of developing each apartment has nearly doubled, to $540,000. Dozens of projects are lined up for an additional $850 million in future state funding. Federal tax credits, which the state oversees, will bring even more money to bear.
Yet one thing has remained constant: The public isn’t allowed to see the details of how all these dollars are being spent.

Oregon is one of the only states in the country with a carve-out in its public records law that prevents disclosing the financial details of subsidized housing projects, thwarting researchers and journalists who have tried to examine their costs.

The issue is especially pressing in the Pacific Northwest, where leaders have tied the lack of affordable housing to the region’s dire homelessness crisis. Understanding and controlling the cost of construction could make it possible, with the same amount of money, to either build more rent-restricted apartments or to discount rents more steeply.

Margaret Van Vliet, a former director of Oregon’s state housing agency, told ProPublica that lawmakers should revisit the exemption. Despite all the state’s spending on housing, Oregon’s homeless population continues to grow.
“For all the public money, we seem to be digging a deeper hole,” Van Vliet said.
In other states, researchers and journalists have used developers’ financial records to investigate spiraling costs of subsidized housing.

Los Angeles Times reporters in 2020 revealed that the cost of some low-income housing units in California had grown to more than $1 million each , driven in part by government rules that pushed construction prices higher. The Times found that 12,000 more low-income families could have received homes between 2011 and 2015 had costs been as low as they were elsewhere.

Researchers from the University of California, Berkeley showed earlier this year that California was spending $300 million a year just in development fees on subsidized housing, enough to have financed another 1,250 apartments each year. In July, California Gov. Gavin Newsom signed legislation that aims to slash those fees.

A study published last year and co-authored by Jason Ward, an economist who directs the nonpartisan Rand Corp.’s Housing Center, compared the costs of constructing subsidized housing among California, Texas and Colorado, finding that California’s highest-in-the-nation prices were driven by requirements to pay “substantially above-market wages and unusually large architectural and engineering fees.”
If California had Colorado’s production costs, the study found, it could have built four times as many rent-subsidized apartments.
Those types of analyses are impossible to perform in Oregon.

Ward said Oregon’s secrecy is difficult to defend. He said cost information about subsidized housing is typically public. In his research, he said, he’s gotten such data from 17 states and been denied it only in New Jersey.

“When you’re just looking at how public funds are used, there should be an incredibly strong bias towards transparency,” he said. “And when you see costs going up and up and up and the outcomes aren’t good, there’s an almost unqualified public case that these things should be open to scrutiny by taxpayers, policymakers, the media, whomever.”
Oregon’s Legislature approved the exemption in 1997, when Oregon’s state housing agency had a staff and budget that were both one-fifth what they are today.
State housing officials warned about the consequences of revealing the finances behind low-income apartment projects.
“Not that we’re concerned that there’d be something in there,” Lynn Schoessler, then the deputy director of Oregon Housing and Community Services, told lawmakers in a public hearing.

But Schoessler said there could be problems if the public were allowed to see detailed financial information that developers submit to the state while applying for funding. Disclosing the records might “give somebody an indication whether this corporation was ripe for takeover or a buyout or whatever,” Schoessler said in a hearing. “So we’re concerned on the corporate level.”
Lawmakers almost unanimously agreed to exempt the records from disclosure.
Not all details about subsidized housing in Oregon were made secret.

The Portland area’s regional government, which manages a local low-income-housing bond, publishes the costs of projects the bond has funded, showing some units have reached $900,000 apiece. And fine-grained cost information may be obtained, on request, if the project is run by a public housing authority like Portland’s. But these account for just 20% of the subsidized housing units that Oregon is building. The bulk are sponsored by private developers and funded through the state housing finance agency, Oregon Housing and Community Services.

Although the state agency will divulge how much a developer said a project would cost when it applied for funding, it redacts the itemized expenses — things like the costs of construction materials, the contractor’s profits or the fees paid to lawyers, brokers, loan agents, developers and the state agency itself.

A spokesperson said the agency knows the cost per unit, per square foot and per bedroom for each development it has subsidized. But the state said that information, which would allow the public to see which projects were the most expensive, is not subject to disclosure.

Oregon has a sunshine committee that reviews public records exemptions and identifies ones that should be rolled back. Charlie Fisher, its co-chair, said the committee should examine the low-income housing carve-out.

“Verifying how public dollars are being spent, especially at this scale, is one of the fundamental reasons why people should have access to public records,” Fisher said. “Given the amount of money we’re talking about, the case is even stronger.”
The secrecy mandate in state law shrouds more than just the financial details of a project.

When we requested financial records for three apartment projects around Portland, the agency redacted a list of languages spoken by the tenants that a developer hoped to attract. In application material for that developer’s project, the agency also redacted the plan for translating tenant outreach brochures from English. And it blacked out an explanation of any financial risks the project might face, along with the developer’s plan for covering cost overruns.

It turns out that the developer, in this case, was Home Forward, the Portland housing authority. The local agency released a copy of its application material to ProPublica without redactions, revealing mundane details the state had tried to keep secret. Here’s a sample of what Home Forward identified as the project’s financial risks: “market volatility, site-specific challenges, and unforeseen design modifications. Economic factors such as inflation, material price fluctuations, and labor shortages could impact overall construction costs.”

A spokesperson for the state said the information about languages and financial risks was redacted because the public records exemption shields “market studies and analyses” as well as pro forma statements, which show a development’s anticipated cash flows.

Andrea Bell, the state housing agency’s director, said in an emailed statement that she is committed to transparency and expects her agency to be open, accessible and accountable to the public. But she said she takes seriously the agency’s responsibility to comply with the exemption in Oregon records law for housing financials.

Asked to comment on whether she supported the exemption and thought it was necessary, Bell said in a statement: “The cost of construction is a topic of growing interest. We will take your request under consideration as we assess ways to proactively share construction costs so that they are more readily available to the public.”

In the meantime, the agency charged ProPublica $130 for the cost of collecting and redacting the documents it provided us. It denied our request to waive the fees, saying that “the interest of the general public would be better served by preserving public resources.”
Transparency hasn’t slowed development in other West Coast states.

In California, where the financial details of housing projects are public records, the funding remains highly competitive, with more than half of shovel-ready applications being turned away because demand exceeds available funding. “We have not encountered any difficulty in developing affordable housing because those documents are public,” said a spokesperson for the California state treasurer’s office.

In Washington state, officials have repeatedly released financial information about the housing projects they’ve funded to developers, researchers, media and other members of the public. A housing official there said developers know the information is open to the public, and it hasn’t been an issue.
ProPublica asked the Washington counterpart of Oregon Housing and Community Services for financial documents for three projects around Seattle. They were released without redactions — and for free.

paras: The Eater Seattle Heatmap aims to answer the question “Where should I eat right now?” for people trying to keep up with the city’s constantly changing dining landscape. It focuses on newer restaurants — typically opened or revamped significantly within the last six months or so — that are reshaping Seattle’s food scene for the better.

In July 2026, we added hot new “not a New York deli” Louie’s , Okonomiyaki Jiban-Ya , from the minds behind Ginger and Scallion and Secret Congee, and sleek Fremont tapas bar Balandra . articles.title: The Best Seafood Restaurants in Seattle
articles.author: <name>Mark DeJoy</name>
paras: Seattle is synonymous with seafood, and anyone who visits from out of town naturally wants to know where the city’s best seafood is. But that’s a tricky question. There are some self-described “seafood restaurants,” but fish and shellfish work their way into nearly every menu around Puget Sound. This includes oysters on the half shell at too many happy hours to count, crab and geoduck served as high-end delicacies, and sandwiches where freshly caught salmon or tuna is the star ingredient. A “best seafood in Seattle” map would pretty much just be a map of Seattle. So consider this a sampler platter of some of what the city has to offer across several different styles of cuisine and price point.

articles.author: <name>Meg van Huygen</name>
paras: Often thought of as Seattle’s southern little sister, Tacoma has surged in population in the last decade, and Washington State’s third-largest city can definitely hold its own against its siblings when it comes to its food scene. From fried chicken and waffles in Lincoln to luscious bagel sandwiches in Edison City, from Vegas-style fine dining in rural Midland to the absolute ocean of Korean food in Lakewood, the dining options here are tremendous. And don’t forget the beer, gothic vegan Cuban food, and the destination Vietnamese barbecue. Hungry? Don’t sleep on Grit City.

articles.title: An Eater’s Guide to Seattle
articles.author: <name>Sophie Grossman</name>
paras: Seattle is nestled in one of the most beautiful regions of North America. On clear days, you can look west over Puget Sound to see the Olympic Mountains and east across Lake Washington to the Cascades. The metro area is home to immigrant communities from all over Asia as well as Mexico, Central America, Ethiopia, and Somalia; there is also a substantial Indigenous population here. The cultural and ethnic diversity, combined with the wide range of local ingredients, makes the area a fertile ground for restaurants.

Owning a restaurant is a financially risky proposition in the best of times, and area owners are struggling with rising costs, especially now that the tipped minimum wage has expired in Seattle . But that hasn’t dampened the creativity of local chefs: 2025 saw a wave of exciting restaurant openings, and noteworthy new spots are always popping up . Here is a guide to the city’s ever-changing dining scene.

Washington is an agriculturally rich state, and Seattle restaurants benefit from an abundance of nearby farms, fruit orchards , fisheries, shellfish farms , ranches, and wineries . But the city is most famous for its seafood. Salmon is such a part of the area’s culinary identity that in the past, Sea-Tac Airport literally rolled out a red carpet for the first Copper River salmon of the season to arrive from Alaska. Shellfish is a Seattle staple, with many places serving oysters plucked out of its surrounding cold, nutrient-rich waterways. One local delicacy-bordering-on-novelty is the humble geoduck (pronounced “gooey duck”), an enormous clam that sometimes catches newcomers off guard because it looks like a penis.

Seattle features many great cuisines but is perhaps known best for its Asian restaurants. The city has an exceptional Japanese food scene and is home to world-class sushi masters — most notably Shiro Kashiba — and sustainable sushi pioneers like Taichi Kitamura. Pho is ubiquitous around town , and teriyaki — that sticky-sweet Japanese American dish — is a Seattle specialty, popularized by Toshihiro Kasahara at Toshi’s Teriyaki Restaurant in the 1970s (Kasahara still makes teriyaki at his latest restaurant, which is up north in Mill Creek). The Chinese restaurant scene is diversifying to include more regional cuisines, such as Sichuan . Bubble tea is also ubiquitous, and you can find some excellent options at old-school spot Seattle Best Tea or the University District location of Taiwanese chain Don’t Yell At Me . (The U District runneth over with bubble tea.)

But perhaps the hottest cuisine in Seattle is Filipino. Filipino immigrants have lived here since the 19th century, and Pike Place institution Oriental Mart is a testament to the longtime influence of Filipino cuisine. However, in the past half-decade, there’s been an explosion of innovative restaurants, like Melissa Miranda’s Musang and Aaron Verzosa and Amber Manuguid’s Archipelago (the latter of which was nominated for a 2025 James Beard Award ). There is also a bevy of buzzy but more casual Filipino-influenced spots, like the Chicken Supply , Moto Pizza , Hood Famous Bake Shop , and Ludi’s Restaurant .
Eater publishes plenty of maps detailing the top places and things to eat and drink in Seattle. Here are a few of our most popular guides to help you get started:

New Restaurants: This list changes every two months and includes restaurants that have opened or reopened in the last six months. Right now, notable new spots include the biang biang noodle champion Lily Wu’s waterfront seafood boil spot, Happy Crab ; Pioneer Square pastry shop and summer soft-serve stop the Pastry Project ; and new-wave Italian American restaurant Uncle Dom’s Italian Kitchen .

Essential Restaurants: If you need to narrow down the quarterly guide to Seattle’s 38 standout dining destinations even further, you might start at Off Alley , a 14-seat restaurant in a renovated brick alleyway in Columbia City, with its hyper-seasonal French-inflected small plates, excellent natural wines, and punk rock soundtrack. For something more casual, head to 40-year-old Beacon Hill standby Billiard Hoang for some of the city’s best pho and banh mi, plus a round of pool. Renee Erickson’s Sea Creatures restaurant group has come to define PNW cuisine in the past couple of decades, and her oyster bar, the Walrus and the Carpenter , is a must-visit. And you can’t forget about Communion , the soul food restaurant in the Central District from chef Kristi Brown.

Bakeries: One underrated aspect of Washington State’s agricultural prowess is the high-quality wheat that’s grown here. That local flour fuels an abundance of creative bakeries , some of which straddle the line between bakery, coffee shop, and restaurant, like Saint Bread in the University District, which was named a top bakery in the U.S. by the New York Times in 2024, and its sister cafe, the Wayland Mill . Some draw on Scandinavian baking traditions, like Queen Anne’s Byen Bakeri , while others are Asian-influenced, like the CID’s Fuji Bakery and Paper Cake Shop in Fremont, where you can get slab-style sheet-cake slices. Ben’s Bread in Phinney Ridge is a sourdough destination, and on Wednesday nights, it serves pizza that reliably and justifiably draws a massive line (you can only place an order in person).

Bars: Seattle’s bar scene is marked by countless dives , elegant cocktail lounges, and everything in between . Cocktail standouts include James Beard-semifinalist Rob Roy ; Canon , which features the nation’s largest spirits list; and Zig Zag Café , a Pike Place Market bar and restaurant where the Last Word, a famous cocktail, was reintroduced to the world by bartender Murray Stenson . And Pacific Inn , which is famous for its fish and chips , the Central District’s Twilight Exit , and Ballard institution Hattie’s Hat are some of the city’s most treasured dives. Seattle also boasts wine bars and bottle shops galore , like La Dive , a playful Capitol Hill hub for natural wine, and Le Caviste , which feels like a little slice of Paris bistro culture in Downtown Seattle.

Breweries: There’s been an exciting proliferation of breweries throughout Seattle in recent years, but Holy Mountain , with its constantly changing menu of offbeat, barrel-aged beers, is a must-visit. Cloudburst , just north of Pike Place Market, is a masterful maker of award-winning IPAs . Many breweries, too, have become hosts for Seattle’s many thriving food pop-ups , particularly Ballard’s Fair Isle Brewing . Relatively new entrant Project 9 Brewing has drawn acclaim for its wide array of beer styles, while Bizarre Brewing ’s complex, low-ABV brews have quickly become a mainstay among day-drinking beer dads.

Coffee: Seattle’s coffee shops run the gamut from lived-in hangouts that have been there for decades to trendy, new-wave espresso spots focused on lighter roasts and more diverse flavor profiles. Recently, a young generation of coffee lovers has brought renewed appreciation for Vietnamese-style phin-brewed coffee, which you can find at places like Hello Em and Phin in the International District, Coffeeholic House in Columbia City, and Fremont’s Aroom , which recently opened a second location on the city’s newly revitalized waterfront. Coffee originated in East Africa, and several spots around town are rooted in the deep-seated coffee traditions from that part of the world. You can experience an Ethiopian coffee ceremony at Lands of Origin in Pike Place Market, try specialty single-origin brews at Avole , or grab an excellent cup at one of Boon Boona ’s many locations around the city.

Views: You can’t help but notice the sparkling scenery in and around this fetching city, but some restaurants boast particularly stunning views . Ferry across Elliott Bay to dine on Hawaiian-Korean creations at Marination Ma Kai or nab an Adirondack chair on the north end of Lake Union for oysters and a skyline view at Westward .

Pike Place Market: If you’re visiting Downtown Seattle or taking a tour of the city with out-of-towners, chances are you’ll end up at Pike Place at some point . While Pike Place might have a touristy reputation, don’t let that deter you. It’s possible to take in the extravagant fish-tossing and partake in some of Seattle’s best food, whether that be the aforementioned lo-fi Filipino dining pioneer Oriental Mart or ultra-dramatic Italian American restaurant, the Pink Door , with its spinach lasagna and occasional trapeze artists.
These are the key areas of the city every self-proclaimed food lover has to survey — complete with what to eat and drink in each.

Capitol Hill is Seattle’s historically LGBTQ neighborhood and a nightlife hub. Though it’s contending with gentrification , it’s still home to many colorful queer businesses. It’s also one of Seattle’s best dining neighborhoods. See some of the finest options in our neighborhood guide . For Mexican, don’t miss Carmelo’s Tacos ; for Laotian, see Taurus Ox , which now has a burger-only spinoff restaurant, Ox Burger . A relative newcomer to the neighborhood, Ramie is making some of the most exciting and innovative moves in haute Vietnamese cuisine at the moment. If you are in the market for a high-end experience, Lark is a fine dining restaurant that is still doing it right, while LTD Edition Sushi is one of the city’s top omakase counters.

The Chinatown-International District (also known by shortened names like the CID, the International District, or the ID) is home to Chinatown, Japantown, Filipino Town, and Little Saigon, as well as too many incredible restaurants to name here. See our neighborhood dining guide for tons of options. For something more immersive, the Wing Luke Museum runs a food walking tour that is a great opportunity to learn about the rich history of the CID through the lens of its diverse cuisine. Gan Bei is a perfect late-night hangout for beer, Chinese fried chicken, and sausage clay pots, while Saigon Vietnam Deli is a great spot for a quick banh mi. The Thai restaurant E-Jae Pak Mor is famous for its dumplings with paper-thin skin . Don’t forget Tai Tung , Seattle’s oldest Chinese restaurant, founded in 1935. But for many locals, the top reason to go to the CID is the massive Asian supermarket Uwajimaya , which sells an array of products and also has plenty of hot food counters and a food court.

Once a rough-and-tumble Scandinavian fishing village, 21st-century Ballard is now startlingly hip. The neighborhood — mapped out for your dining convenience — straddles the line between modern development and the preservation of its early history. There’s plenty worth eating here, including wood-fired pizza perfectionist Delancey and Lebanese restaurant Cafe Munir . Little Beast , Eater Seattle’s 2025 restaurant of the year , takes English pub food to new heights with its meticulously sourced and prepared meats. The neighborhood also has its own brewery district with more than a dozen brewers within walking distance, including Reuben’s , Stoup , and Urban Family .

Georgetown has a history of grit and brick, but has also become a thriving culinary and cultural destination, fostering a local character that draws in visitors from all over town. You can find decadent slices of cakes at Deep Sea Sugar and Salt , wonderful vegan sandwiches at the divey Georgetown Liquor Company , top-notch handmade pasta in a romantic setting at Mezzanotte , and intricate six-course prix fixe meals at the Corson Building .

This eclectic neighborhood (see: massive troll under a bridge ), just north of Lake Union, and to the east of Ballard, harbors a fair share of standout restaurants: Chef Mutsuko Soma’s soba destination Kamonegi , the French-ish Le Coin , and Local Tide , where people line up for the succulent crab rolls, in particular. James Beard Award-winning chefs Rachel Yang and Seif Chirchi run the kitchen at Joule , known for its kalbi short ribs, local pickled vegetables, and a fresh take on Korean cuisine. If you want something sweet, check out Doce , which serves massive brioche-style doughnuts and has quickly expanded to three locations since opening in 2023 .

West Seattle’s dining scene and the picturesque Alki Beach are equally impressive. You’ll find inventive dinners using hyper-local ingredients at Driftwood , fantastic pasta in a century-old log house at Il Nido , and top-notch smoked meats at Lady Jaye , which also boasts a terrific backyard patio. Seafood fans should check out Mashiko for sushi that emphasizes sustainability; those recovering from a long night can eat breakfast (or get some hair of the dog) with a side of killer soundtrack at Easy Street Records & Cafe .
Central District , U District , Tacoma , and Seattle-Tacoma International Airport .

It’s a hot dog or sausage slathered in — wait for it — cream cheese and grilled onions. The murky origin story goes back to the late 1990s, when a bagel cart in Pioneer Square went a little rogue . Though it sounds strange, the sweet and meaty flavor combination is surprisingly satisfying (try some hot sauce on it), and even high-end restaurants will sometimes riff on the concoction for specials. You can generally find a Seattle dog at Capitol Hill stands bumping Latin dance music and selling the franks late into the night along with elotes, and at other hot dog-focused places around town .

This sticky-sweet Japanese-American dish is a Seattle specialty, popularized by Toshihiro Kasahara at Toshi’s Teriyaki Restaurant in the 1970s. You can still find Kasahara north of the city at Toshi’s Teriyaki Grill in Mill Creek; within Seattle city limits, try gluten-free options at West Seattle’s Grillbird Teriyaki .

Old-school yet relevant, Canlis is Seattle’s archetypal fine dining restaurant, which has shown a great deal of versatility over the years. In 2025, the restaurant shook up its ownership structure (now the sole owner is Mark Canlis) and suffered a much-talked-about negative review in The Seattle Times . But whoever is at the helm, Canlis remains one of the city’s most important restaurants.

This James Beard Award-winning chef channels rustic European country cooking by way of seasonal Pacific Northwest ingredients in her bright, airy, elegant spaces. She runs some of the city’s most adored spots through her Sea Creatures restaurant group, including oyster bar, the Walrus and the Carpenter, and Westward . Despite controversy over staff unionization efforts , which coincided with the closure of several restaurants in 2025, her empire continues to grow: She recently opened three new restaurants in Pioneer Square, Lowlander Brewing , Un Po Tipsy , and Mio Oh Mio . Meanwhile, her innovative Capitol Hill steakhouse Bateau, which has been closed since summer 2025, has rebranded as Jeffry’s and recently reopened with a similar menu.

A legend in his own right, this beloved chef trained with Jiro Ono (of Jiro Dreams of Sushi ) before bringing Edomae-style sushi to Seattle and defining the scene here over the past 50 years. He spent early days at Maneki and other spots around town, pioneering the use of local seafood, then two decades at namesake Shiro’s . Finally, after the world’s shortest retirement, Kashiba returned to the counter in late 2015 at Pike Place Market’s Sushi Kashiba , where you can still find him on Wednesdays and Saturdays. He’s now focused on helping the next generation of Seattle sushi chefs open their own restaurants.
